#6471. For Over a Decade, They’ve Been the Face of the World’s Most Entrancing Treasure Hunt. Have They Finally Solved Oak Island’s Mystery?

There's gold in the water on Oak Island—but a maze of old tunnels is hiding where it’s coming from.

“Hundreds of thousands of dollars and the wits of the cleverest American engineers and college professors have been vainly spent in trying to solve the mystery of the Money Pits of Oak island and its sheltered haven, Mahone bay, Nova Scotia.”

Those words appeared in the pages of Popular Mechanics 100 years ago, in the March 1926 story “Hunting Hidden Treasures.” In the century that followed, the amount of money and wits expended on the mystery of Oak Island has only grown.

Since 2014, the public faces of the Oak Island mystery have been Rick and Marty Lagina, the stars of HISTORY’s long-running series The Curse of Oak Island. Across more than 250 episodes, audiences have followed along with the brothers’ success and setbacks, their obsession and their frustrations. When they began, via an investment in Oak Island Tours in 2006, they were pursuing a quixotic dream inspired by an old magazine article, joining a pantheon of prospectors that included Hollywood stars like Errol Flynn and John Wayne, and at least one U.S. President (Franklin D. Roosevelt, who kept tabs on the developments on Oak Island throughout his life).

Now, heading into their fourteenth season (debuting on November 10 on the History Channel), the siblings from Michigan are striking a more retrospective tone, reflecting on their role in this centuries-long quest for answers and the colleagues they’ve lost along the way (the season premiere pays homage to the late Dan Blankenship, a longtime partner of the Laginas who spent more than 50 years searching Oak Island before his 2019 passing). Now, there’s a question that’s become just as pressing for the two men as the Oak Island mystery itself: “After all these years, what was it all for?”

Ahead of the new season, Rick and Marty Lagina sat down with Pop Mech to reflect on fourteen seasons of television, how treasure-seeking has changed over the centuries, and what keeps them, and audiences, returning to Oak Island and its mysterious Money Pit year after year.

Although the marketing for Season 14 has leaned heavily on a new discovery through which the Laginas’ “lifelong quest has finally paid off,” the brothers kept the details of the coming episodes close to the vest. (Pop Mech was able to preview only the season premiere.) Otherwise, they were as candid and at times as self-effacing as they’ve been throughout fourteen seasons of television.

In fact, Rick is quick to dispel what he feels is the biggest misconception fans of the show often have. “We’re portrayed on some level as experts in every field, and we’re not,” he told us. “That’s why we have such a large tent of people helping us, because we’re not experts in every field, every arena.”

“It’s a very complex mystery,” he adds, “and we need everybody under the tent, if you will.”

That tent doesn’t just include the various experts who appeared on the program over the last decade, but also the centuries of treasure hunters who came before them. “Rick holds those prior searchers in this huge, high regard,” Marty says of his brother, “and thinks about them all the time.”

If one believes the account published in The Yarmouth Herald in 1863, that list of prior searchers stretches all the way back to 1795. That’s when a young farmer named Daniel McGinnis arrived on Oak Island via canoe, propelled by a piece of folklore which claimed that Captain Kidd had buried millions of dollars worth of treasure on the island. As he searched, he came across a depression in the ground that seemed deliberate, and called together a small team to dig on the site. As they excavated to a depth of 30 feet, they found remnants of a previous presence at the site (some accounts say flagstones, others oak platforms), and that led them to think they’d discovered the location of the buried treasure—or what’s long been referred to as the “Money Pit.”

In the early 1800s, the Onslow Company reportedly paid a visit to the same site, and they dug deeper into the Money Pit than McGinnis ever dared to go, roughly 80 to 90 feet deep. The Onslow Company found further indications that the pit was deliberately dug to store something, though their evidence was far more destructive. Their dig set off a booby trap that caused the Money Pit to flood with seawater up to the 33-foot level. The Onslow Company was unable to bail out the excavation site at the time. To make matters worse, Marty would note, later attempts only exacerbated the problem.

“There was almost certainly a flood tunnel that caused the initial booby trap,” he told us, “And people will come up to you and they’ll say, well, why don’t you shut off the water this way or shut off the water that way. The problem is there’s been so much pumping over the years by other people that the water is coming in from other places.”

Marty, who possesses an extensive engineering background in both petroleum and renewable energy, is both enamored with and exasperated by what’s been left behind by the treasure hunters who preceded him.

“From an engineering standpoint, I’m always astonished, absolutely astonished and in rapt admiration for what those people were able to do with picks and shovels,” Marty says of those earlier excavators. “I mean, you can’t believe it. If you were out there, and you saw these hand hewn timbers come up from 180 feet down. They had nothing. They had horses, you know? I mean, it’s just really amazing.”

Impressive as that work was for its time, it left modern-day diggers with consequences of their own.

“One of our scientific consultants, Ian Spooner, is a PhD geologist. He calls it Chutes & Ladders,” Marty says, before quickly adding, “He actually calls it Snakes and Ladders, because that’s the Canadian thing.”

“We have so many interconnected passages now that have been made by other people that we have to decipher all that,” he laments, “And every time a timber comes out, I mean, almost every time, you have to say, is this an original worker’s timber or is this a searcher’s timber? And we have to run the scientific analysis on that.”

In the show’s ninth season, water samples from the site turned up trace amounts of gold, a discovery that showed just how badly booby traps and centuries of earlier digging had muddied the trail.

“If you followed [the show], you know there’s gold in the water, which has kept us coming back for years,” Marty continued, “Now it’s there, it’s real, it’s coming from a source. And if the water was just moving geologically, like I’m used to in my prior business, we could trace it back, but the problem is it’s all interconnected, so it’s difficult.”

Have past attempts to solve the mystery actually further obscured Oak Island’s secrets? Did stories stoking the hunger for treasure actually, if unintentionally, contribute to the partial destruction of the Nova Scotia island?

If so, it’s a guilt that Pop Mech partially shares.

At one point in our conversation, Marty cuts in to jokingly ask, “By the way, can I do a quick commercial for Popular Mechanics?” to which this author, never afraid of a little self-promotion, gleefully assented. “Growing up, I loved that magazine. Absolutely loved that magazine,” he says, “And Rick will attest, we kind of had a hard time getting our hands on actual magazines. But I mean, I would read those from cover to cover.”

“There is one connection to Popular Mechanics too, aside from our interest in the magazine,” Rick chimed in to add, “There was an article in Popular Mechanics about Oak Island.”

As it turns out, there was more than one. But if Rick recalled an Oak Island story from one of the magazines he and Marty read cover to cover, it was likely the one published at the exact mid-point between 1926’s “Hunting Hidden Treasures” and today.

Fifty years ago, the September 1976 issue of Popular Mechanics ran with the cover story “7 Great Quests of Man,” and the mystery of Oak Island’s treasure was discussed alongside such cryptic quandaries (and just plain cryptids) as Bigfoot, the Loch Ness Monster, ancient aliens, and Noah’s Ark.

But if such outlandish company makes the Oak Island mystery feel like a fantasy, the work the Laginas have done over fourteen seasons has pulled things back into the realm of reality. While a literal pot of gold at the end of this proverbial rainbow would be a satisfying conclusion, Rick says that the true value of these excavations extends beyond the potential payday.

“When you talk about story, the science and technology has pushed the timeline of what happened on Oak island, or at least when something started to happen on Oak Island, to me, has been pushed back, literally, into the latter part of the 13th century,” he noted, “We have core samples from wells, we have carbon dates from old walls, we have archaeo-astronomical alignments. I don’t see any other explanation that some of these structures, including Nolan’s Cross, given the alignments contained within them, were of that time frame. So what happened long, long ago, well before Europeans were supposed to be on this continent, to me, that’s a story in and of itself.”

Perhaps, in that sense, the treasure has served as the profit motive, the lure that funded centuries of expeditions, which may finally be uncovering the site’s true history.

“Marty has always said that the mystery of Oak Island has endured because of treasure, because of that component, and he’s absolutely right,” Rick concluded. “But at this point, I think the treasure and the story are somewhat aligned in terms of importance, and I hope that we can push forward on both agendas.”

The new season of The Curse of Oak Island premieres on the History Channel November 10 at 9/8c.

#6470. Mexican Seafood and Natural Wines Are in the Spotlight at This New NYC Restaurant

A stacked tuna tostada, puckering shrimp aguachile, and more seafood dishes stun at El Camarón Peludo

Known for their roasted and slow-cooked meats at Taqueria Ramirez, Tania Apolinar and Giovanni Cervantes partnered with chef Carlos Barrera to open a new seafood-focused wine bar this year. Here’s what a full day of prep looks like at El Camarón Peludo in the West Village.

First, fresh shrimp from Sinaloa, Mexico; Ecuador; and more locales are de-shelled and de-veined for three central shrimp dishes. Then, Cervantes starts the fresh salsa for the day, taste testing and comparing each batch to the salsa from last week to make sure the flavor is consistent. A bright red salsa is mixed with mayo to create the sauce on the camarones zarandeados, a shrimp version of a fish dish from the Pacific coast of Mexico that is usually grilled in a flat wire grill basket.

Upstairs, Apolinar prepares the wine bar for opening, laying out chilled seafood on ice in the window and wine bottles that will be placed in chilled buckets for service. She recommends sitting at the long, winding bar to watch the bartenders and chefs work.

Back in the kitchen, Barrera starts breaking down Spanish tuna for a creative tuna tostada layered with spicy mayo, fish eggs, habanero-lime oil, avocado, and crispy leeks. Then it’s taco prep, including the pescadilla (a deep-fried fish taco) and a shrimp taco with queso fresco, refried beans, and slices of roasted poblano peppers. Cervantes and Barrera prep the raw bar area, making salsa verde and salsa negro. The green salsa is made with parsley while the black salsa is layered with habaneros, piquin chile, and squid ink.

Cervantes explains that his original idea to pair the innovative seafood plates with bubbly wine turned into a natural wine bar, with El Camarón Peludo sourcing bottles from all over the world.

Using machine learning, astronomers developed a new way of looking at James Webb telescope data that allows far-off planets to emerge from their stars' glare.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When it comes to spotting planets orbiting distant stars, the biggest hurdle is often separating the signal from the noise — specifically, trying to distinguish a planet from the stellar glare around it. That's true even for the most sophisticated telescopes, including the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

Now, astronomers have developed a new way to spot planets that were formerly drowned out in a sea of light. Using a combination of modeling and machine learning techniques, they picked out a previously hidden giant exoplanet in data from JWST. The results were published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

"Planets are a million times fainter than their stars," study first author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, an astronomer at Northwestern University, said in a statement. "So, to image exoplanets, we need to remove that glare."

Telescopes like JWST use instruments called coronagraphs to block out some of this excess light, similar to the way the moon and a pinhole camera operate during a total solar eclipse. But even the best coronagraphs have limitations — for example, they can't block all the glare, and the telescopes themselves move.

Even the most stable telescopes vibrate almost imperceptibly as they collect light, so the images a telescope produces contain ever-so-slight mismatches compared with what the instrument actually sees. These slight shifts can be enough to obscure even very large exoplanets.

To address this, Ferrer-Chavez and his team developed a "digital twin" of JWST that virtually recreates how light travels through the telescope's detectors, minus any movement-based imperfections. To fine-tune this digital replica, the researchers used computational models based in real-world physics alongside machine learning techniques similar to those used to train AI. But the authors stressed that this is not an AI model.

"Because we already know the physics, we don't need AI to understand what's happening," study co-author Jason Wang, also an astrophysicist at Northwestern, said in a statement.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers named their approach Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets, or FLIP.

Using FLIP, the team analyzed data from three stars, including 51 Eridani, which is located around 97 light-years from Earth and was already suspected to have a giant exoplanet orbiting it. Although the planet, called 51 Eridani b, had been detected by ground-based telescopes, it was drowned out by light in previous JWST observations. With FLIP, however, 51 Eridani b popped out from the dataset.

The scientists hope this approach will help astronomers pick out even more hard-to-spot exoplanets, especially ones that look like the planets in our own backyard. In the nearly 35-year history of exoplanet hunting, the vast majority of planets we've found have been radically different from those in our own solar system, partially because larger and more reflective worlds are easier to spot with current telescopes.

"It's not that [solar-system-like planets] don't exist," Ferrer-Chavez said. "It's that we can't see them."

Ferrer-Chavez, R., Wang, J. J., Bouman, K. L., Freeman, W. T., Pueyo, L., Feng, B. Y., & Perrin, M. D. (2026). Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit. Nature, 659(8139), 58–62. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11213-z

#6468. Nearby Dwarf Galaxies Show Surprising Lack Of Oxygen, Says Paper

Vital to almost all life as we know it, oxygen has long been valued as a tracer of the chemical evolution of the of the cosmos. As such, it provides a practical means of tracing how the heavy elements of iron, carbon, nickel, magnesium and sulfur --- the real building blocks of habitable planets like our own --- are distributed throughout the galaxy and beyond.

In a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal, researchers using Hubble studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies â small galaxies containing a few thousand to hundreds of millions of stars â and found that much of the oxygen they expected to see is missing, says NASA.

For the first time, we have measured both how much oxygen produced by stars in low-mass galaxies remains in those galaxies, and how much oxygen has been lost from those galaxies throughout their lifetimes, Grace Telford, the paperâs second author and an assistant professor at the University of Utahâs Dept. of Physics & Astronomy, told me via email.

The findings show that dwarf galaxies can hold onto only a small fraction of the oxygen made by stars, says NASA.

The team used Hubble Space Telescope data; data from NASAâs retired Spitzer Space Telescope as well as the ground based Very Large Array and Australian Telescope Compact Array, NASA notes.

Most of the oxygen does come from core-collapse supernovae, which are the explosive deaths of massive stars, says Telford. Yet a very small fraction is also produced in other types of supernovae caused by the remnants of low-mass stars becoming unstable or merging, she says.

As the cosmosâ third most abundant element, oxygen is relatively easy to detect and measure, and its production is well understood â making it a reliable indicator of how chemical elements are distributed in a galaxy, says NASA.

We found that typically 15 percent of the oxygen produced by stars in these low-mass galaxies is still found inside those galaxies today: mostly in their gas, but small fractions are also in the stars and dust, says Telford. The explanation is that energetic radiation from massive stars and their deaths as supernovae drive oxygen-rich gas out of the galaxies over time, she says.

This means that the missing oxygen is likely in the gaseous halos surrounding the galaxies. That is, the Circumgalactic Medium (CGM). This missing oxygen has also likely traveled even farther into the intergalactic medium.

The Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds (GLOW) project, jointly funded by NASA and the National Science Foundation, is a large-scale effort to understand how gas and heavy elements move between low-mass galaxies, their CGM, and the intergalactic medium.

To do this requires combining a large set of new and archival observations of low-mass galaxies from both ground-based and space telescopes, says Telford.

The idea is that most of the oxygen found outside these dwarf galaxies has been driven there by energy from massive stars and supernovae explosions.

Similar measurements of oxygen (and other heavy elements) lost from galaxies have been made for massive galaxies like the Milky Way, says Telford. But low-mass galaxies are expected to lose oxygen more easily due to their smaller gravity and our paper demonstrates that this is indeed the case, she says.

In the Milky Way, there is about one oxygen atom for every 2,000 hydrogen atoms, says Telford. In low-mass galaxies like those in the GLOW project, that value is more like one oxygen atom for every 10,000-20,000 hydrogen atoms, she says.

The GLOW project found that low-mass galaxies lose more oxygen than current galaxy formation simulations predict, implying that we donât yet have a complete understanding of how massive stars interact with their host galaxies, says Telford.

#6467. A Stellar Odd Couple at an Unusual Stage of Evolution

Most of the stars in the Milky Way are what we might call normal stars. They're main sequence stars like our Sun, meaning they're doing what most people probably think stars do: shining as they fuse hydrogen atoms into helium atoms on a vast scale.

But all stars run out of hydrogen fuel eventually, and some stars end up in odd states as they evolve off of the main sequence. White dwarfs represent one of these odd evolutionary statea. Our Sun will become one of these when it runs out of fuel in several billion years. These stars are super-compact and dense; they're about as large as Earth but have about as much mass as the Sun. They shine only with remnant energy.

White dwarfs are strange, but not rare. About 97% of the Milky Way's stars will become white dwarfs eventually, and they're not difficult to detect.

Another strange end-state is the neutron star. They form when massive stars explode as core-collapse supernovae. Since massive stars are rare, so are neutron stars. They're also extremely dense objects, but even more dense than white dwarfs. They can have 2 solar masses and be only 12 km in diameter. It's often said that a teaspoon of neutron star would 'weigh' one billion tonnes.

Not only are neutron stars rare, but they're difficult to detect; they're small, dark, and cold. But some neutron stars do announce their presence as pulsars. Pulsars are rapidly rotating neutron stars that shine beams of light from their poles. If one of those beams is aimed at us, astronomers can see it blinking. They're cosmic lighthouses.

Millisecond pulsars (MSPs) are a specific type of pulsar with rotation periods of 10 milliseconds or less that only form when they have a binary companion. It happens when the companion swells up due to its own evolution. Mass spills over from the companion and spirals onto the millisecond pulsar, giving it angular momentum, or rotational energy that makes it spin rapidly. Finding these binary stars is of great interest to astronomers, and a team of researchers from Italy and Germany have found one with a very young white dwarf partner.

Their research is published in a paper titled "The youngest white dwarf companion to a millisecond pulsar: Insights from NGC 362D." It's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics, and the first author is Greta Ettorre, a PhD student in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the Alma Mater Studiorum University of Bologna, Italy.

Globular clusters are excellent hunting grounds for millisecond pulsars, because the stellar density is so high that neutron stars are more likely to have companions. NGC362D is a millisecond pulsar with a rotation period of only 5.83 milliseconds, meaning it rotates more than 10,000 times per minute. It was first discovered in December, 2022, in the globular cluster NGC 362, about 29,300 light years away.

*Somewhere in this globular cluster (NGC 362), a millisecond pulsar and its binary companion, a white dwarf, are in a rare stage of evolution. The pulsar, which is a dense, rapidly spinning neutron star, has been drawing material away from its less dense white dwarf companion, hastening its evolution into a white dwarf. Image Credit: By ESA/Hubble, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?

"Millisecond pulsars (MSPs) form in binary systems containing a slowly rotating neutron star (NS) that is eventually spun up to millisecond periods by heavy-mass and angular-momentum transfer from an evolving companion," the authors explain. "The recycling scenario for MSP formation predicts that the mass transfer between the non-degenerate companion and the NS typically starts when the donor is either a main sequence or a subgiant or red-giant branch star."

The pulsar's companion, called COM-NGC 362D, is the youngest MSP companion ever found. It's a proto-white dwarf, which indicates that it's only just entering the earliest stages of becoming a white dwarf. "Our analysis robustly shows that this object is a very low-mass (â¼0.18âMâ) He white dwarf (WD) still in the pre-cooling phase," the authors write.

NGC 362D and its companion are important because the astronomers caught them in a rare stage of their relationship. "Interestingly, a detailed comparison with updated binary evolution models indicates that this object completed the mass-transfer phase only recently (â¼0.6 Gyr ago), thus strongly suggesting that COM-NGC 362D is the youngest WD companion to a MSP identified to date," the authors explain. This is especially interesting because as the pulsar draws material from its companion, it drastically shapes the companion's evolution, forcing it to become a white dwarf far sooner than it would on its own. This is called the recycling process.

Astronomers found COM-NGC 362D by cross-referencing radio data from the pulsar itself with ten years of Hubble observations in ultraviolet and near-infrared. By comparing that data with stellar evolution models, they determined its age and other properties. But there was something else: the same models showed less UV radiation than expected for a white dwarf like this. Something was blocking or attenuating some of its UV.

"Remarkably, in this respect, the photometric properties of NGC 362D show, for the first time in this class of objects, significant wavelength-dependent variations that are consistent with the presence of residual circumstellar material," the authors write. This material was likely expelled during the mass-transfer phase, emphasizing how young the white dwarf is.

âWhat makes this system particularly interesting is the possibility of observing it at a very early stage of its evolution,â lead author Ettorre said. âMoreover, the attenuation of the signal that we observed in the ultraviolet could indicate the presence of material still surrounding the white dwarf.â

They acknowledge that it's unclear if the material could've survived for this long, but it's still their preferred explanation.

The purple line in this figure shows the reference model for a young He white dwarf in its cooling phase. The pink points are fitted data from COM-NGC 362D. (The blue points represent data that couldn't be fitted for technical reasons.) "The observed trend, with larger deviations at shorter wavelengths, is consistent with a self-extinction effect likely produced by circumstellar material surrounding the proto-WD companion," the authors write. Image Credit: Ettorre et al. A&A, 713, L14 (2026)

"Our proposed scenario envisages that COM-NGC 362D is an extremely young WD that only recently ended the mass-transfer phase and is surrounded by a residual cloud of material producing self-extinction," the authors write.

This means that they system is a unique opportunity to study the aftermath of the recycling process that generates an MSP. If COM-NGC 362D has only recently had its outer layers stripped away, then the dense core left behind is only in the early stages of transitioning to a white dwarf. So finding this young core could make it easier to identify others.

âNGC 362D currently offers us a unique opportunity to study what happens in the immediate aftermath of the millisecond pulsar recycling process,â said study co-author Emanuele Dalessandro, a researcher at INAF. âIn this context, the possible presence of material around the white dwarf is particularly interesting. In fact, it could produce signatures at radio wavelengths in addition to the optical, similar to those observed in systems with non-degenerate companions, and could therefore help us correctly interpret the properties of other young systems.â

Though their proposed scenario is that COM-NGC 362D is a very young white dwarf at the end of the recycling process, they do acknowledge another possibility. "Alternatively, the material may have been expelled during a previous hydrogen-shell flash," they write.

In any case, pulsars are fascinating objects, and their rapid and regular pulses of electromagnetic energy make them natural clocks. This makes them useful in studying other aspects of the Universe. Understanding how they form will only be helpful.

âMillisecond pulsars rotate with extraordinary regularity and can be used as true natural clocks. Measuring the arrival times of their pulses with extreme precision allows us, among other things, to study gravity under extreme conditions and to carry out increasingly precise tests of general relativity. Understanding their surroundings and reconstructing their evolutionary history is therefore essential to fully exploit what these remarkable cosmic laboratories can tell us.â Ettorre concludes.

#6466. A Common Food Emulsifier Could Solve One of Rocketry’s Oldest Fuel Problems

In propulsion system design, engineers have long faced a trade-off between solid and liquid rocket fuels. Each has advantages and disadvantages, and in an effort to try to min/max the efficacy of different types of fuel, researchers have long placed an emphasis on a hybrid between solids and liquids - in other words theyâve been working with gels. Unfortunately, gels have their own sets of problems to deal with. But a new paper published by Pranay Mudaliar and Jerin John of Concordia in the journal Langmuir uses an uncommon ingredient to elegantly solve some of those problems, but which is typically used in a completely different area of human activity - lecithin.

Solid rocket boosters, like those that powered the Space Shuttle, are very stable, durable, and quick to ignite. However, they are also impossible to turn off - you have to burn through all the propellant at once.

Liquid fuel, on the other hand, is much more flexible, much like automotive fuel. Liquid fueled engines can be throttled up and down, restarted multiple times, and generally are much more controllable than their solid cousins. However, they also float and slosh around in tanks, which is a particular problem in zero-gravity environments, as that sloshing can cause vapor pockets that can break a turbopump if not filtered out beforehand. Liquids also have a tendency to leak or evaporate over long periods, making them less than ideal for multi-year journeys through the solar system.

Fraser talks about some of the difficulties of orbital refueling.

On paper, gels offer a great solution to that. While sitting in a tank, they would act like a dense solid, but can also act like a liquid when forced into a combustion chamber. However, they suffer from their own challenges, such as shelf life and temperature dependent phase changes.

The paper details a new type of fuel that uses an unexpected special ingredient. Lecithin might sound familiar, but not in the context of rocket fuel. Itâs commonly used as an emulsifier in food. Itâs commonly used to keep chocolate smooth, and salad dressing cohesive, and can be found on thousands of supermarket food labels. In the context of rocket fuel, lecithin acts simply as an organic gelling agent.

When combined with a trace amount of calcium chloride salt, lecithin molecules self-organize into microscopic worm-like structures called micelles. Chains of these form an invisible 3D mesh that can trap and hold kerosene molecules, a more traditional type of rocket fuel, in place. Lecithin also has the added advantage of being an organic compound made up of carbon and hydrogen, so it will burn right alongside the kerosene rather than acting as simply dead-weight like may other non-combustible thickening agents previously used to create gel fuels.

Scott Manley talks about the engineering behind solid rocket boosters. Credit - Scott Manley YouTube Channel

But perhaps the most interesting feature of the new fuel is a physical phenomenon known as shear thinning. When the gel is sitting under normal conditions in a tank, it holds it shape firmly like a gelatin, eliminating the sloshing features that cause so many problems in liquid-fuel rockets. However, as soon as thereâs a mechanical pressure or shear force applied - such as when the spacecraft pressurizes the fuel lines - the micellar mesh breaks apart, causing the gel to temporarily quickly collapse into a liquid.

Measurements detailed in the paper show the gelâs viscosity dropping by a factor of more than 100, creating an easily pumpable liquid that can be sprayed through injector nozzles. But when the pressure stops, the material snaps back to its rest state as a gel. There are also two other environmental stimulants that can cause this liquid transformation - if the gel is heated up to between 59 and 68 degrees C, or splashed with a small amount of ethanol. In other words, localized thermal or chemical triggers could easily intentionally force specific amounts of fuel to liquefy without requiring the bulk of the fuel to do so.

Another appealing feature of the gel, from an experimental standpoint anyway, is that itâs clear. Therefore researchers can watch it with optical high-speed cameras and lasers to analyze its structure as well as its spray patterns. And a final appealing feature is its shelf life - the gel stayed stable in a tank for over a year, with no visible signs of a phase separate that plagues many other gelatin-like fuels.

It is still a very long road from the benchtop to the launchpad though. The new fuel hasnât actually been sprayed through the high-pressure injectors that would be used on an actual rocket engine. Nor has it shown that itâs capable of withstanding the vibrations and temperature shocks that come from being launched into space. But as the Concordia researchers continue its development, this new gel is looking promising for potentially powering a future mission.

Concordia University - RESEARCH: New gel fuel could make rocket and satellite propulsion easier to control

P. Mudaliar & J. John - Rheology and Thermal Characterization of Lecithin-Based Kerosene Gels for In-Space Propulsion

UT - A New Non-toxic Propellant is Looking Promising

#6465. Best Knife Set After Years of Testing Knives (2026)

I’m just going to say it: You don’t need an 18-piece knife block with a blade for every conceivable kitchen task. If you find one of those sets out in the wild, what you’ll probably find is that a lot of knives in the block still have a factory-sharp edge, because they’ve never been used. At the same time, it’s hard to ignore the sheer value a lot of knife sets offer. For most home cooks, buying every knife piecemeal is akin to adding a 15%–20% tax.

After testing dozens and dozens of knives and talking with our Test Kitchen editors and professional chefs, the consensus is that the best knife set really only needs three essentials: a chef’s knife, a bread knife, and a paring knife. As you get more confident or curious in the kitchen, you might choose to add a versatile nakiri knife, a handy petty knife, or a versatile cleaver, but we generally recommend doing so on an ad hoc basis with an eye for how it will fit into your cooking and how much you truly want to spend on a knife.

When it comes to the core pieces of a knife set, though, many of the best knife makers make great versions of multiple knife types. In that spirit, the sets here offer high performance and great value without compromise. Nearly every knife recommended in these sets has been tested individually, so I feel confident saying you’ll be happily slicing, sawing, and coring with every recommended option.

Read on for our top knife set picks, including a couple of slightly more expansive options with a knife block and steak knives for those who want some extra pieces.

New in this update: Editors spent some extended time with our top picks and we’ve added their long-term user notes.

Individual Mac knives have come out on top in our testing time and time again for their high-quality construction, ultrasharp blades, lightweight feel, and middle-of-the-road price point. This three-piece set is made up of a chef’s and petty knife that are the top overall picks in their respective categories, and a bread knife that’s essentially a luxe version of our favorite serrated knife.

In testing, the Mac Professional Chef’s Knife was versatile and comfortable to use thanks to its ergonomic pakkawood handle, able to work through a giant mound of veggies efficiently without making our hands cramp up. Its blade was one of the sharpest we tested and combines the best qualities of Japanese- and Western-style chef’s knives in both its material and shape. Made of molybdenum high carbon steel, it strikes a balance between the brittle (but extra-sharp) steel used in Japanese blades and the softer, more durable steel typical of a Western knife. Similarly, its shape is a hybrid of the rounded edge of a Western-style blade and the straighter edge of a Japanese knife.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, we are also big fans of Mac’s Professional Series petty knife, and for similar reasons: It’s razor-sharp and offers a unique shape that splits the difference between a utility knife and paring knife.

The bread knife included in this set is also part of Mac’s Professional Series. It’s a tier up from the Superior Series knife that won our bread knife test, which is evident in its build quality: While it features the same scalloped blade of the Superior Series knife, it has a metal bolster that makes for a more seamless connection between the blade and handle, and a more balanced overall feel while slicing.

In the long run: I used these Mac knives for more than a year (the chef’s knife I used for five) and they served me well the whole time. The paring knife is on the long side so it’s better suited to things like cutting hard cheeses than peeling or coring, though I prefer using a Y-peeler and an apple corer anyway. But because it’s longer, it was also easier to sharpen. The bread knife is perfect. The shape of the serrations and curve of the blade provide excellent leverage, and because they’re wavy instead of pointy, I didn’t notice loss of sharpness at all. It’s also heavy enough that its weight helps me push through without tearing.

And then there is the chef’s knife. The old standby, loved by every reviewer and Test Kitchen editor who has tried it. The balance, weight, and shape made it versatile, and the steel sharpened fantastically. However, after a couple years, my Mac did chip. I was able to resharpen and salvage it, but I’m not the only one who ended up with a chipped blade. The Mac we kept in house for long term testing also chipped after a few years. As reviewer Jesse Raub has noted in a number of his knife pieces, Japanese knives like the Mac are made from harder steel, so they don’t dull easily but they do chip. Personally, I find it one of those trade-offs you have to make when you’re picking a knife, and there is much good about the Mac that I still happily endorse it.

If you like the high-end look of beautiful Damascus steel and prefer a more rounded belly to your chef’s knife (better for rocking chops on the board), this set from Shun may be the one for you. Shun’s knives consistently perform well in our testing, and each of these knives has earned a spot as a top pick in its category. And by buying them as a set, you’ll save a modest amount of money off the total cost of the individual knives.

One of the things that sets Shun’s Classic line apart is that it features the brand’s proprietary VG-MAX core, a high carbon steel with additional metals like chromium and molybdenum added in the mix to help with corrosion resistance and sharpness. In testing, we found this made for blades that cut effortlessly through anything we threw at them and retained their sharpness over time.

The rounded pakkawood handles of the Classic line knives made each of them extremely comfortable to hold, and because the handles maintain an even thickness throughout their length, they allow each user to find the grip and hand positioning that’s best for them.

Shun’s knives are routinely some of the sharpest in our testing, and we appreciate the more Western-leaning hybrid shape of their blades. It makes them great options for anyone who wants the versatility of a Western chef’s knife while looking for the precision edge of Japanese gyuto. While Shun’s bread knife is a little short for our tastes, it was also the sharpest and easily sliced through everything during its round of testing, earning it a top pick in that category.

In the long run: I’ve had these Shun knives for a year now, and they’re my go-to set. The chef’s knife is incredibly comfortable to hold. A smooth notch where the blade meets the handle gives me a comfortable spot to pinch-grip, and the handle fits my small hands. The blade’s shape lets me glide and rock through tough ingredients. The paring knife is sharp and precise enough to hull strawberries but sturdy enough to cut into a thick wedge of Manchego. At nine inches, the bread knife handles most sourdough miches with ease, though I occasionally wish it were a little longer for really wide ones.

Renaissance 5-Piece Knife Set With Magnetic Board

Spending $400 on a knife set, like the Mac and Shun options above, is a big investment, even if you’re getting three high-quality blades. For a more budget-friendly alternative, we recommend this four-knife set (it gets called a five-piece set because the knife board counts as a piece) from Mercer Culinary’s Renaissance line. It’s a great cheap option for anyone who wants reliable knives without committing to a premium price point.

Mercer’s knives have consistently performed well in our testing, from the Renaissance line to the more affordable Genesis and Millennia collections. Their Millennia 10-inch Wavy Edge Bread Knife, priced under $16 when bought on its own, is even one of our top picks. In our tests, the Mercer chef’s, bread, and paring knives all delivered clean, consistent cuts and maintained their edges well after repeated use. While they didn’t outperform our favorite pricier knives, they came surprisingly close considering they were less than half the cost. Made from high carbon steel with full-tang construction and durable handles, the knives in this Renaissance set feel solid, well-balanced, and easy to control.

While we prefer the Japanese petty knife over a Western utility knife shape, there’s enough value in the core three knives of this set that we think it’s worth it for anyone who wants an affordable refresh or is stocking their kitchen for the first time.

In our testing for the best chef’s knives, Hedley & Bennett’s chef’s knife stood out as well-balanced, comfortable to grip, and easy to maneuver thanks to the seamless transition between the handle and blade. After months of use, our Test Kitchen editors were impressed with how well it held up. And while testers preferred the Mac, if you’re looking to bring some fun color into your kitchen while still investing in a high-performing knife set, Hedley & Bennett is a great choice.

This set includes a utility knife rather than a paring knife. It’s about two inches longer than a traditional paring knife (5.6 inches versus 3.5), making it a bit more versatile for larger tasks, such as slicing an oversized apple.

The bread knife is on the shorter side, at only 8.6 inches, but its sharp, tapered serrated edge allows for more controlled, precise cuts than some straight-blade designs. Deputy Food Editor Hana Asbrink notes that the blade’s slope also helps prevent your knuckles from hitting the cutting board, a common issue with bread knives that maintain the same width along the entire blade.

While they aren’t the sharpest knives out of the box, they’re made of high carbon stainless steel and can be easily sharpened to a finer edge. While we think most home cooks would like this set, its biggest advantage is the variety of colorways, which make for a more aesthetically pleasing kitchen.

In the long run: I’m in a less-is-more phase of my life, mostly because my shoe box of a kitchen leaves little room for 10 knives. So the pared down three from Hedley & Bennett fits perfectly in my space. They’re lightweight and the tapered spines have contributed to a welcome feeling of precision when using them. The chef’s knife gets the most use—there’s something rhythmic about slicing garlic with it. But the utility knife has come in handy more often than I thought. I’ve used it, along with my trusty kitchen shears, to break down whole chickens. And the angled tip of the serrated knife has made it useful for more than sawing through crusty bread. The blade shape helps for more delicate work like piercing tomato skin without mangling it.

With use, a few minor scuffs and scratches have started to show. My colleagues have also warned me that the handles can crack over time, though that hasn’t been an issue for me over the first several months. Bless the greater knife powers that be. I do make a point of never leaving my knives in the sink and always drying them thoroughly after washing.

—Nina Moskowitz, associate cooking editor

The Wüsthof Classic line helped define high-end knives both at home and in professional kitchens for decades. Over the years, Wüsthof Classic set the standard for what to expect for performance and durability—full-tang construction, high carbon stainless steel, and a razor-sharp edge that’s easy to maintain. In our tests, Wüsthof’s 8" chef’s knife has been a standout for many years, and the included bread knife and paring knife are also great options.

The big catch is that many cooks prefer the more nimble Japanese-style and hybrid knives, and Wüsthof’s heritage puts its Classic line in a more expensive bracket. Still, if you prefer the heft and durability of Western-style knife set, it’s hard to go wrong with this one—and they’ll last a lifetime with good upkeep.

If you’re looking for a more expansive knife set beyond our essential three-piece recommendation, Shun’s Classic line stands out. This seven-piece set includes the core trio—a chef’s knife, paring knife, and bread knife—plus two smart additions: a 6-inch petty knife and a pair of herb shears. The petty knife fills that sweet spot between a paring and a chef’s knife, perfect for tasks that need more precision than a big blade allows but would overwhelm a smaller one, like slicing citrus or trimming proteins.

The herb shears are a surprisingly handy upgrade. Instead of dragging out a cutting board just to mince some parsley or chives, you can snip them straight into a salad, soup, or garnish. Still, this is a good example of where a large set can sell you short: herb shears are less versatile than a standard set of heavy-duty kitchen shears.

The set also comes with a honing steel to keep your knives sharp and a sleek 11-slot bamboo storage block, which gives you extra space to add other styles down the line, like a nakiri for vegetable prep, a santoku, or even a cleaver.

In the long run: By jumping up to the larger seven-piece set I got to add my favorite part of the set: the herb scissors. I use them to snip parsley right over a finished dish without pulling out a cutting board. They’re small, but they can still cut raw chicken into chunks when I don’t feel like reaching for a knife. Just be sure to hand-wash and towel-dry them right away. If you leave them dripping wet, they will get watermarks.

Large knife sets that come with a storage block are handy—it’s literally a one-stop shop. And if you’re a fan of serving grilled ribeyes whole to your guests, you’re going to need some sharp steak knives. Global’s knives are strong performers in our tests, and their unibody construction makes them easy to clean and maintain. We also like their unique steel, which retains sharpness without being as brittle as other alloys.

While they can be polarizing, many people find their dimpled steel handles comfortable to hold, and their knives come sharp out of the box. A big reason we like this large set over other options is that larger knife sets are usually extremely expensive, or they’re made up of a knife maker's budget line. Here you see strong value for great knives, and the inclusion of a petty knife, a chef’s knife, and a kiritsuke-style slicing knife means there’s nothing you won’t be able to cut with swiftness and precision.

Given its size, it’s a well-balanced set, and the inclusion of the serrated utility knife is a nice touch for slicing tomatoes or peeling squash. It may feel like a hefty sticker price, but you’d be hard-pressed to find this many high-quality knives at this price point from other brands.

In the long run: While the Shun knives are my home set, the Global Chef’s knife is the one I always use when I’m working in the Test Kitchen. The balance and the size of the knives in this set (a slightly shorter chef’s and bread knives) are perfect for smaller women. Other BA editors have echoed this idea in the past. The secret is in the handle. Its dimpled steel gives you a secure grip, and it starts wide before tapering in, which makes it perfect for small hands. It feels hefty (it’s full of sand) while still being lightweight, which matters when you need to stay nimble with your knife cuts.

We’ve been testing knives for years now, and we have found that the same brands tend to come out on top across each knife category. Luckily for you, aspiring knife set purchasers, that means we’ve had no trouble finding three-piece sets from brands we know and love that feature product-test-winning, quality knives our team of experts can vouch for. Each set listed above is made up of individual knives we’ve tested against a long list of competitors and wholeheartedly approve of.

Head over to our individual reviews of the best chef’s knives, best bread knives, and best paring knives for even more information.

How many knives do you need in a knife set?

We firmly believe that three knives are all you really need: a chef’s knife, a paring knife, and a bread knife. Together, they cover just about every essential kitchen task, from chopping vegetables to slicing crusty loaves.

That said, if you’re looking to upgrade or expand your collection, three additional knives are excellent additions: a nakiri knife, a petty knife, and a cleaver. While not essential, they’re nice to have: the nakiri offers extra precision for vegetable prep, the petty knife is ideal for those in-between tasks that a paring or chef’s knife might not handle quite as neatly, and a cleaver can help tackle larger chopping tasks (or precision cuts with a Chinese cleaver).

Mac has come out on top of our knife testing across the three core knives—chef’s, serrated, and paring—but the question itself is sort of like asking “who is the best guitar player.” Different people will find different knife shapes, weights, and handle styles better or worse for their hands. And, there are a lot of small elite knife makers out there that make items that aren’t just kitchen tools, but works of art. If you want to investigate some of those, we’d encourage you to check out a shop like Chubo Knives for elite Japanese blades.

But as far as affordable, widely available knives go, Mac’s routinely outperformed the competition. They are made in Japan from molybdenum high carbon steel, which blends the durability of Western-style steel with the precision sharpness of traditional Japanese blades. The result is a knife that’s lightweight, versatile, and sharp. Mac’s bread knife took the top spot in our testing thanks to its 10.5-inch blade, which is an inch and a half longer than most. That extra length makes it easier to slice through wide loaves like focaccia in a single stroke.

We stand by all of our recommended knives, but what you will get if you buy higher-end knives are blades made from better steel that are finished with more care. That means they’ll hold an edge longer, require less sharpening, and last for years with proper care. For most home cooks, it’s worth investing at least $150–$200 in a chef’s knife since it’s the blade you’ll reach for every day. Secondary knives like paring, bread, or utility knives don’t need to be as pricey, but if you use them often, it may be worth upgrading those too (and getting them as part of a bundle in a small knife set is a good way to do that).

Read more here about how much you should spend on a knife.

Is it better to buy knives individually or as a set?

It depends on your priorities. The great part about a knife set is that it’s a one-and-done purchase. You get the three essentials (chef’s, bread, and paring knives), and you can trust that each knife in the set has been tested to perform at a high level. That said, buying individually gives you more flexibility. Maybe you prefer a 6-inch chef’s knife over an 8-inch or a longer bread knife like Mac’s 10.5-inch version over Shun’s 9-inch or Hedley & Bennett’s 8.6-inch tapered blade. Think of a set as a strong starting point: It gets you well-equipped right away, but you can always mix and match later as you learn what sizes and styles feel best in your hand.

In general, yes—most manufacturers will offer at least some discount when you buy knives as a set rather than one at a time. How much of a discount? Well, that varies. For some brands, buying a three-piece set is like getting a third knife for free. For others, you might only save a few bucks. Still, many sets will also go on sale, adding even more savings to the already discounted knives. At the end of the day, it’s worth pricing out each knife in a set to see how much you’ll save by buying the bundle, and weigh that against being able to pick your favorite knife from each type. Still, we find that if you’re a fan of one knife from a brand, you’ll probably enjoy the handle style and comfort of other knives from the same brand—combined with some savings, you get a strong argument for picking out a knife set when you need a kitchen refresh.

What’s the best way to store your knives?

Proper storage is just as important as proper sharpening when it comes to keeping your knives in good shape. No knife should ever be tossed into a drawer with other utensils—that’s a quick way to dull the edge, damage the blade, or worse, hurt someone.

The best storage option depends on your kitchen setup and preferences, but our favorite is a magnetic strip mounted on the wall. It keeps blades accessible, protects the edge, and works for all shapes and sizes, whether you’ve got a slim paring knife, a hefty cleaver, or even kitchen shears. Another big plus: magnetic strips take up zero counter or drawer space and are easy to clean with a quick wipe. These are our favorite magnetic strips.

Jesse Raub: I’ve been a professional kitchen product tester since 2021, where I tested nearly everything: espresso machines, wooden spoons, bread proofing baskets, pizza stones, garlic presses, and more. My fascination with kitchen knives began in 2003 when the chef at the kitchen where I worked let me use his personal Wüsthof knives during prep work one day. Over the last two years, I’ve tested over 70 different knives for Bon Appétit and written about the best knife sharpeners and how to best sharpen your knives at home. If you’re ever on the phone with me and hear a light scraping noise in the background, just know that I’m likely touching up my kitchen knives on a whetstone and testing their sharpness by slicing sheets of paper.

Additional testing by Olivia Tarantino and Noah Kaufman

#6464. The 50 Best Restaurants 2026: The Full List of Winners

Congratulations to Asador Etxebarri in Spain, named the World’s Best Restaurant of 2026

Tonight, the 50 Best Restaurants 2026 were announced at a ceremony in Lima, Peru, with Basque Country restaurant Asador Etxebarri crowned the new top slot on the list. Bangkok tasting counter Gaggan was ranked No. 2, Copenhagen’s immersive, 50-course experience Alchemist was No. 3, Mexico City’s Quintonil No. 4, and Hong Kong’s Wing No. 5, shuffling most of the top rankings from last year. New York City’s Atomix was the only U.S. restaurant to make the 50 Best Restaurants.

Of the specialty awards, Singapore’s Lesley Liu received the Best Sommelier Award (sponsored by Vik), Ghana Food Movement was given the Champions of Change (sponsored by illycaffe), Yiaga in Melbourne was named the One to Watch, Doris Lam received the 50 Best Restaurants Scholarship Award, Jessica Rosval of Al Gatto Verde was named Best Female Chef (sponsored by Lexus), Thailand-based Dej Kewkacha was Best Pastry Chef (sponsored by Sosa), Atomix’s Junghyun Park was given the Estrella Damm Chefs’ Choice Award, and Ferran Adrià was given the SevenRooms Icon Award.

Just as a review, U.K.-based media company William Reed launched the 50 Best Restaurants lists in the early 2000s, publishing the first World’s 50 Best Restaurants list in Restaurant magazine in 2002. The 50 Best gained greater fame in the 2010s, with the top spot going to the likes of Noma (Copenhagen, Norway), El Celler de Can Roca (Girona, Spain), and Osteria Francescana (Modena, Italy). The organization made the wise decision in 2019 to move each year’s winner to a separate “Best of the Best” list — a sort of hall of fame for takers of the top spot — giving new restaurants the opportunity to take the crown. Since then, Geranium in Copenhagen (2022), Disfrutar in Spain (2024), Central (2023), and Maido (2025) in Lima have earned the No. 1 ranking. Noma qualified as a winner again in 2021 because it had “closed and reopened.”

The 50 has also expanded its reach with multiple regional lists, such as the Latin America’s 50 Best, Middle East and North Africa’s 50 Best, Asia’s 50 Best, the 50 Best Bars (which also has its own regional lists), 50 Best Hotels, and even 50 Best Wineries. The entire brand has reached a level of global reputation and fungibility that rivals something like the Michelin Guide ( which has itself ventured into hotels and wineries). But the 50 Best Restaurants is the granddaddy of all listicles, and the one that draws the most attention and criticism regarding its methodology and alleged pay to play. One vocal critic, chef Ana Roš of Hiša Franko in Slovenia, announced earlier this year that she would not attend the ceremony, a move commenters like Top Chef judge Tom Colicchio lauded.

The polling is conducted anonymously among more than 1,100 voters, a mix of industry professionals, food writers, and “well-traveled gourmets,” with at least 25 percent turning over annually. Each voter nominates 10 restaurants in order of preference, up to six in their home region and at least four outside it. The rankings are just a pure tabulation of those votes.

The organization has made efforts to clarify its voting and ranking policies, stating that any restaurant can qualify and that what constitutes “best” depends on each voter. The 50 has also expanded its awards to consider diversity and inclusion, recognizing female chefs (which itself has raised eyebrows), sustainability, sommeliers, pastry chefs, hospitality, and Champions of Change, an award that “celebrates and recognizes unsung heroes” who are “driving positive change in their communities.”

Last week, the “back half” of the list, also known as 51-100, was announced, with the only U.S. restaurant, SingleThread (Healdsburg, California), ranked at No. 93. On the 2025 50 Best Restaurant list, New York’s Atomix was the only U.S. restaurant to make the top 50, ranked at 12. Perhaps in order to remedy the dearth of U.S. and Canadian restaurants on the World’s list, the 50 (the organization previously known as 50 Best), commenced North America’s 50 Best Restaurants in the fall of 2025. Atomix topped that list, followed by Mon Lapin (Montreal), Restaurant Pearl Morissette (Lincoln, Ontario), and other U.S.- and Canada-based restaurants.

#6463. An Artificial CORTEX to Guide Satellite Rescue Missions

The growing problem of satellites crowding one another is generating concern in the space community, for good reason. Almost 20,000 satellites orbit Earth now, and with more satellite constellations and other satellites being launched every year, Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) is starting to look like it's reaching its limit. Of particular concern are the 3,500+ plus satellites that are basically zombies. They are either completely non-functional or not sending any signals alerting other satellites to their presence.

A collision between two satellites could be catastrophic. Satellite constellations have some built-in redundancy which would help deal with the loss, but there's an additional risk. A collision could also create a debris cloud, multiplying the ongoing risk. The Kessler syndrome describes a cascade of collisions generated from debris created in a single, initial collision, that goes on to create even more collisions. It's like a feedback loop that keeps getting worse.

Somehow, this problem must be dealt with. The existing debris is one thing, but intact zombie satellites are another. These have lost the ability to communicate and warn other satellites of their presence. These can be repaired, and that's the subject of new research in Acta Astronautica. It's titled "CORTEX: An autonomous, end-to-end, convex-based framework for close-range rendezvous trajectory design and guidance with hardware testbed validation," and the lead author is Minduli Wijayatunga, a new aerospace engineering faculty member in The Grainger College of Engineering, at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

This work is all about the growing idea of Rendezvous and Proximity Operations (RPO). Spacecraft docking operations have been custom-designed solutions for individual situations, like docking with the ISS. But with thousands of zombie satellites, custom docking solutions aren't realistic.

"Rendezvous and Proximity Operations (RPO) are shifting from bespoke demonstration missions such as Northrop Grummanâs Mission Extension Vehicles, Chinaâs Tianyuanâ1, and Astroscaleâs ADRAS-J, to routine missions due to the growth of in-orbit assets and the resulting demand for inspection, servicing, assembly, and debris mitigation," the authors write. They point out that while there were only about 13,700 tracked objects in LEO in 2019, there were more than 24,000 in 2025. That's a shocking increase, and there's no signs of it slowing down.

That's forcing scientists to develop autonomous ways to deal with the overpopulation. The growing population of satellites isn't the only thing dictating an autonomous solutions. Autonomous repair is also critical because of the time delay in communications between the ground and LEO, and because satellites are best observed in and maneuvered with in windows when they're illuminated by sunlight.

âThese spacecraft must be able to track the trajectories of uncooperative objects autonomously but also make go/no-go decisions without waiting for the ground to decide,â Wijayatunga said. âSuppose your thruster fails or you encounter high-order orbital perturbations that push you away from your nominal trajectory. In those instances, how do you make those decisions?â she added.

That's what CORTEX is being designed to do.

"This paper presents CORTEX (Convex Optimization for Rendezvous Trajectory EXecution), an autonomous framework for close-range rendezvous trajectory design and guidance under sensing, actuation, and dynamics uncertainties," the authors write.

"Among RPO phases, the close-range rendezvous, where the servicer locates the docking port axes and approaches the client, is particularly safety-critical. It must satisfy strict operational constraints (e.g., keep-out zones, approach corridors, plume/line-of-sight constraints, illumination/eclipses) under limited actuation authority and imperfect relative navigation," the authors write.

Wijayatunga's PhD involved trajectory and guidance using something called convex optimization. Convex optimization is a method that lets a spacecraft approach a target using math and trajectories, not input commands. It basically solves a math problem of trajectories and thruster commands until the lone, best answer is arrived at. The answer should mean a successful docking. The idea is to reach that docking state with minimal fuel use while also following constraints like the targets no-go zones or keep-out zones. Those are places on the target satellite that might house sensitive equipment like sensors or antennae.

This work expanded to include the idea of sunlight windows. Cortex also includes options other than aborting if things went sideways. Instead of calling the docking off, CORTEX can reconsider its options. It even takes into account situations that arise where thrusters can't be fired.

âI wanted to bring that same idea into developing CORTEX and expand it, taking into consideration sunlight windows so we don't have to operate in darkness. That, and the replanning versus abort architecture, are novel in CORTEX,â Wijayatunga said.

âCORTEX has trajectory design and guidance, so if you deviate significantly from your nominal mission trajectory, it replans the trajectory and re-approaches unless you are in severe violation of your keep-out zone, in which case it returns to a passively safe orbit. It's an algorithm to recover from the unexpected. We tried instances where you're supposed to use your thrusters, but you can't for whatever reason. And CORTEX was very robust to that.â

CORTEX is being tested in a particular modelled docking scenario. It's what's called an ISAM, an In-orbit Servicing Sssembly and Manufacturing. It's designed for what will most likely be fairly typical in the future. It involves a Client Spacecraft Object (CSO) in LEO and is designed to test autonomous approach, servicing, and inspection of the CSO by a servicing spacecraft with a Guidance Navigation and Control (GNC) system for proximity operations.

Hold positions are an important part of CORTEX. In the modelled scenario, there are two of them that let the servicing spacecraft pause and re-evaluate in a fixed relative position. One is at the beginning of the fly around, and the other is at the start of the final approach. They are there to let the servicer pause during eclipses, a new idea in CORTEX.

This figure shows some aspects of CORTEX controlling a servicing spacecraft while it approaches and rendezvous with a client satellite. Blue shows the Rendezvous Sphere, orange shows the Approach Sphere, and red is the Keep Out Sphere. The approach axes is identified as CORTEX's successful solution to the docking problem. Image Credit: Wijayatunga et al. 2026. Acta Astronautica.

One way of looking at CORTEX is as a flow chart governed by four things. "The goals of CORTEX are: (i) minimize fuel and time consumption, (ii) ensure that both the fly-around and final approach occur entirely in sunlight, (iii) avoid the KOS during the fly-around phase, and (iv) satisfy the approach corridor constraint and avoid plume impingement during the final approach," the authors write.

This schematic flow-chart shows how CORTEX works. CORTEX has the ability to abort its approach if necessary, and instead of giving up, it can determine how to re-approach its client. Image Credit: Wijayatunga et al. 2026. Acta Astronautica.

In the tests, the servicing spacecraft was forced into an odd, unexpected situation and CORTEX had to deal with it. Its orbit was unexpectedly perturbed, and thruster operation was impaired, not firing when they were supposed to. Other errors were also introduced, corresponding to unexpected factors like solar storms and thrust errors.

CORTEX fared well in the tests and was able to deal with the unexpected situations in the models. "In all cases, the framework either recovered successfully while respecting safety constraints or executed a safe retreat before entering unsafe regions," the authors write.

âIn some of the hardware tests, if the servicer violates the approach corridor, it leaves the keep-out zone and retreats to a safe position and in others, the servicer is able to recover and carry on with its mission,â Wijayatunga said.

Satellite close approach and recovery isn't purely hypothetical. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAX) launched Astroscale's ADRAS-J in 2024. It successfully maneuvered within 50 meters of a typical piece of space debris, a spent rocket stage, considered to be an 'uncooperative target.' It flew around the object, catching multiple images from different angles. It used sensors and autonomous navigation to accomplish this.

Astroscale's ADRAS-J autonomous spacecraft approached a spent rocket booster, a typical piece of space debris, and captured images of it from multiple angles. It's a step toward eventual servicing of zombie satellites. Image Credit: Astroscale/JAXA.

The hallmark of the past few decades is rapidly-advancing technology. Among other things, it's led to a crowded LEO and a growing population of zombie satellites.

Maybe we'll end up using technological tools like CORTEX, enabled by AI and machine learning, to manage the problems technology has helped generate in the first place.

About half of people with long COVID see meaningful improvement in their symptoms after three years, a new study found.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness.

That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems.

In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame.

This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems.

The new study's findings could help direct the structure of future clinical trials of treatments for long COVID, experts said.

The patients in the study were enrolled in the long-term RECOVER Adult Study. Funded by the National Institutes of Health, the project has recruited thousands of adults across the United States who previously tested positive for COVID-19.

Researchers scored patients based on how they were affected by a range of symptoms, including fatigue, brain fog, shortness of breath and heart palpitations. The study included patients who scored more than 10 points on a 30-point scale — called the 2024 LC Research Index (LCRI) — which attempted to capture these different symptom combinations.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Nearly 1,020 patients met this requirement and were tracked over time; they had in-person appointments and filled out symptom surveys every three months. Scientists marked patients as "improved" once they recorded LCRI scores of 10 or less at two consecutive visits. They found that 36% of the participants had improved two years after their inciting COVID-19 infection, and that figure rose to 50% after three years.

LCRIs hit zero for 26% of the participants after three years, meaning all of their symptoms were gone at the time of the survey.

Reeder said he was careful to avoid describing the participants as "recovered." This decision was influenced by input from the long COVID community to the RECOVER Adult Study, he said. They highlighted that their symptoms can wax and wane, whereas "recovery" implies a permanent resolution. The new study didn't capture, for example, whether individual patients who recorded meaningful improvement later relapsed.

The researchers analyzed which SARS-CoV-2 strain was associated with the most long COVID cases, controlling for patient vaccination status.

Some patients' journeys were far less straightforward than the top-line data might suggest. Although men and women improved at similar rates, adults under 46 were more likely to improve than older participants were. Patients affected by the Omicron variants of SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in 2021 and quickly became the dominant strain of the virus, were more likely to improve than those infected with earlier strains.

Some of the starkest differences in improvement rates were seen between patients with different symptoms.

In a previous study, RECOVER researchers had grouped participants into five subtypes, using an algorithm to connect patients with similar predominant symptoms:

In the new study, patients in the last three groups were less likely to get better within three years. The final group's rate was particularly low, at just 19%.

Dr. Carmen Scheibenbogen, an immunologist at Charité University Medicine Berlin, said these patients' progress resembles that of people with ME/CFS.

"It looks as if at least a major subgroup is suffering from ME-CFS," Scheibenbogen said, noting that COVID-19 may have triggered their condition. "This is a disease which is triggered by different infections, but in the end, the disease [itself] is very similar," she said.

Like long COVID, ME/CFS can affect a wide array of bodily systems, and it remains poorly understood despite recent advances in research.

The team's new findings highlight the need for clinical trials to test possible treatments for long COVID. Both Scheibenbogen and study co-author Harrison Reeder, a biostatistician at Massachusetts General Hospital, said these subtypes would be important to consider in the design of these potential trials.

The multisystem subgroup, Reeder said, "might be a group where an effective intervention can make a bigger difference than people who stand to potentially have a higher chance of improvement regardless."

Future work would need to further scientists' understanding of people affected by long COVID at the level of their genes and proteins, both scientists said.

"There's a lot of work to do in RECOVER and in the world of long COVID research," Harrison said. "There's a lot of opportunity."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.
