#6388. Scientists Discover That Male and Female Hearts Age in Surprisingly Different Ways

The heart may age very differently from one region to another. A detailed study of mouse hearts found that molecular signs associated with chronic inflammation and tissue scarring were concentrated around the aortic valves and aortic root, rather than being distributed evenly throughout the organ.

Researchers at The Jackson Laboratory (JAX) identified these hotspots by mapping thousands of cells from young and aged mice. Published in Aging Cell, the findings suggest that structures often overlooked in cardiac aging research may play a central role in how the heart changes over time.

Previous studies of cardiac aging have largely concentrated on heart muscle, particularly the left ventricle, which pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta and throughout the body. Because mammalian heart muscle cells have very limited capacity for regeneration, understanding how they deteriorate with age has been a major research priority. The JAX team instead examined the entire heart, using single-cell and spatial genomics technologies to identify both the molecular activity of individual cells and their locations within the organ.

“The valves and the major blood vessels are parts often thought of as plumbing rather than the main engine, but this is a very complicated little machine,” said study author Nadia Rosenthal, scientific director at JAX. “It turns out they’re home to many of the cells we’re interested in, and that’s where some of the most important aging-related signals were concentrated.”

“Some of the markers associated with inflammaging were there from the very beginning in young hearts, but they were focused specifically in areas no one had defined before, in the valves and the aorta rather than in muscle tissue,” Rosenthal said. “We really have to think of aging as something that is not linear, because just like we know that people don’t age at the same rate, what we know now is that organs and tissues don’t age at the same rate either, even within one individual.”

Aging is associated with persistent, low-grade inflammation, sometimes called “inflammaging.” The researchers focused on two cell populations involved in this process: immune cells that help regulate inflammation (macrophages) and structural cells responsible for maintaining connective tissue and producing scar tissue (fibroblasts). In older mouse hearts, macrophages showed increased activity in genes associated with inflammation and tissue remodeling, while fibroblasts exhibited molecular patterns linked to fibrosis (or scarring).

“To keep muscle cells happy, the other cells in the heart have to continue supporting them throughout life,” Rosenthal said. “What this study does, for the first time, is provide a comprehensive picture of how those support cells, particularly fibroblasts and macrophages, change with age and contribute to what we call inflammaging.”

The team also detected increased activity in two genes within the identified hotspots. Ccl8 produces an inflammatory signaling molecule, while Cdkn1a (also known as p21) helps regulate the cell cycle and is commonly associated with cellular senescence. Their activity points to changes in signaling between neighboring cells, not simply isolated changes within individual cell types. “We’re not talking about single genes. We’re talking about an entire conversation between immune cells and fibroblasts. As the heart ages, the way those cells communicate changes, and that shift appears to be linked to the inflammation and tissue remodeling we see in older hearts,” Rosenthal said.

Some molecular markers traditionally associated with senescent cells were already present in young mouse hearts. Cellular senescence occurs when cells permanently stop dividing, often following stress or damage. Senescent cells can contribute to inflammation and tissue deterioration, but the researchers found that the presence of commonly used senescence markers does not necessarily establish that a cell has entered this state.

“What surprised us was that some of these markers that have been associated with aging were already present in young hearts. They weren’t where anyone expected to find them, and that forced us to rethink what those markers are telling us,” Rosenthal said. “That turns the usual interpretation of cardiac aging on its ear because these markers alone don’t mean a cell is senescent. There’s nothing senescent about a six-month-old mouse heart.”

The study also identified differences in how fibroblasts responded to aging in male and female mice. In males, older fibroblasts showed greater involvement in molecular pathways associated with fibrosis. In females, aging was linked more closely to pathways involved in heart development and protein production. These findings describe differences in gene activity, not demonstrated differences in cardiac function or disease risk.

Rosenthal noted that cardiovascular disease patterns also differ between men and women, with disease risk generally increasing after menopause in women. However, the mouse findings do not establish a mechanism for those human differences. Comparisons with previously published human heart data did identify several shared molecular programs associated with aging, including pathways involved in cellular stress responses.

“Our findings change the focus from aging across the entire heart to specific anatomical hotspots, helping us better understand how inflammation and fibrosis are connected and which regions of the heart are involved in the aging process,” said study author Amalia Sintou, a postdoctoral associate at JAX.

Age is the leading risk factor for cardiovascular disease, but separating changes caused by aging itself from those associated with lifestyle, environmental exposures, and disease remains difficult. Although the study did not establish whether the identified cellular changes directly impair heart function, the controlled conditions in which the mice lived helped researchers examine the biological effects of aging.

“Valve replacement is common in older adults, and one of the big questions is how much of the underlying damage is driven by aging itself,” said study author Aleksandra Aljakna Khan, a postdoctoral associate at JAX. “Because all of the mice in our study lived in the same environment and ate the same diet, we were able to isolate the effects of aging and show that aging alone can initiate some of these changes in the valves and aorta.”

The researchers are now investigating how exercise, diet, and disease influence the interactions between immune cells and fibroblasts. Their goal is to distinguish changes that occur during normal aging from those that may increase the heart’s susceptibility to disease. Although the current findings do not immediately suggest new treatments, the cellular map provides a foundation for studying how inflammation and fibrosis develop in specific regions of the aging heart.

Reference: “Alterations in the Immune-Fibrotic Axis Are Spatially Localized in the Aging Heart” by Aleksandra Aljakna Khan, Amalia Sintou, Yue Zhao, Antonios Somarakis, Harshpreet Chandok, Juliana Alcoforado Diniz, Ramalakshmi Ramasamy, Gretchen T. Clark, Leon Frommer, Sikander Hayat, Brian S. White, Paul Robson, Ron Korstanje, J. Matthew Mahoney and Nadia A. Rosenthal, 5 November 2026, Aging Cell. DOI: 10.1111/acel.70768

This work was supported by the NIH Common Fund through The Jackson Laboratory Senescence Tissue Mapping Center (JAX-Sen TMC U54 AG079753), with additional support from JAX’s National Cancer Institute-designated Cancer Center (P30 CA034196).

Neuroscientists say people can be "trained" to recognize when they're dreaming — in other words, lucid dreaming may be an acquirable skill.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

During dreams, bizarre scenes you encounter can seem as tangible as reality; you feel as though you're really flying through the sky or being chased through a jungle of bright-purple trees. But in special cases, people realize they're in the midst of a dream as it's unfolding.

Called lucid dreaming, this phenomenon occurs when we suddenly regain our capacity for metacognition, or thinking about our own thoughts, in the middle of a dream. Lucid dreamers can sometimes even control the content or trajectory of their dreams. Now, researchers claim that they've found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they're awake.

In a study involving a few dozen participants, the scientists found that repeating this training twice a week for a month significantly increased how often participants experienced lucid dreaming. They say the approach could have practical applications as an intervention for people with nightmares, anxiety or post-traumatic stress disorder — but those applications are theoretical, for now.

If you could learn how to lucid dream, would you? Let us know in the poll below, and add your thoughts in the comments.

#6386. Scientists finally link human fossils found in China fifty years ago to the Denisovans, early human ancestors that we still know very little about

Two bones from Xujiayao, dug up in China in 1976-79 and dated to 199,000-138,000 years ago, yielded 18 proteins that point to Denisovans.

Between 1976 and 1979, excavators in the Nihewan Basin of northern China recovered 20 human fossils at a site called Xujiayao. From there, it took nearly five decades to tie them to the Denisovan lineage, an extinct human group first identified from DNA in a Siberian cave.

The finds included pieces of skull and jaw and some teeth, buried with animal bones and artifacts that were mostly scrapers and spheroids. Researchers later filed them under five different names.

A team that includes Song Xing and Qiaomei Fu of the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP) in Beijing has now recovered 18 ancient proteins from two of those bones.

One small change in a collagen protein points both to the Denisovan lineage, although the proteins cannot show which Denisovan population the people belonged to.

Uranium-series and electron-spin-resonance dating place the Xujiayao layer at around 199,000 to 138,000 years ago. The first studies noted a thick skull vault and teeth that resembled those of Neanderthals.

Those early descriptions led scientists to call the people Homo sapiens neanderthalensis, early Homo sapiens or archaic Homo sapiens. When the arguments over sapiens stalled, some papers fell back on the neutral term archaic Homo.

A later study of the partial skull called Xujiayao 6 measured a braincase of about 1.8 quarts (1,700 milliliters). That unusually large figure made the skull the type specimen of a proposed species, Homo juluensis, one of several new names listed in a 2024 article in Nature Communications.

The name placed Xujiayao in a group apart from the Homo longi skull from Harbin and from fossils at Dali and Jinniushan. The new paper argues against that divide.

Animal bones from the same layer came first, and they gave a positive result for ancient protein. Next came the human fossils, a right parietal bone from Xujiayao 6 and a piece of the Xujiayao 14 mandible, labeled PA1490 and PA1497 in the lab. Each went through a 3D scan before anyone touched it with a drill.

Researchers in protective gear drilled one small hole in each bone in a clean room at the institute’s Molecular Paleontology Laboratory. They wrapped the surrounding surface in aluminum foil and kept the holes as small as they could.

The powder went into hydrochloric acid and then a 149-degree Fahrenheit (65-degree Celsius) bath for three hours, which split each sample into three fractions.

Empty blanks ran alongside to catch contamination, and the bone of a modern Bactrian camel went through the same steps.

Two labs read the fragments on mass spectrometers, one at Capital Medical University and one at Fudan University in Shanghai.

One software search returned 15,194 unique peptides, the short chains of amino acids that make up proteins, across the two samples.

Old proteins carry a chemical wear called deamidation, and the team used it to separate ancient material from modern traces. Keratins and the trypsin used in the lab showed far less of it.

After further filtering and a check in a second software program, 18 proteins remained, 13 in the skull bone and 15 in the jaw.

The decisive signal sits in COL1A2, one of the chains of type I collagen, the main protein in bone. At position 996, Neanderthals and modern humans carry the amino acid arginine.

Every Denisovan tested so far carries lysine there instead, according to the paper. That reference group consists of two individuals from Xiahe, Penghu 1, the Harbin skull and Denisova 3 from Siberia.

Both Xujiayao bones showed lysine. The skull bone gave 57 peptides with the variant and the jaw gave 61, while each sample gave only one low-quality peptide with arginine.

The researchers then built a family tree from 2,074 amino acid positions in eight proteins, adding Neanderthals, 50 present-day people and a chimpanzee for comparison. Xujiayao grouped with Denisova 3 and other Denisovan-related individuals with a probability above 99 percent.

Xujiayao ranks “among the earliest molecularly confirmed Denisovans,” the authors wrote in Nature. Similar protein work identified a jaw from a Tibetan Plateau cave at Baishiya Karst in Gansu, dated to at least 160,000 years ago.

With the fossils assigned, the team compared their anatomy against other human relatives, using CT scans at a resolution of 37.56 microns.

They took 26 linear measurements, three angles and two indices from the Xujiayao 6 skull. C.-H. Chang shared a 3D model of the Penghu mandible, and X. Wu allowed the scanning of casts from Xuchang and Hualongdong.

Parts of the skull look like Homo erectus. The vault measures 0.30 inches (7.7 millimeters) thick at the top of the head and 0.47 inches (12 millimeters) at the parietal bulge, and the braincase is low and wide.

Other parts look more recent. A strongly arched temporal bone also appears in later species, including modern humans, while the inner-ear layout and, in the Xuchang fossils, a small pit at the back of the skull recall late Neanderthals.

The mix also has its own signature. The authors list a low skull with nearly parallel side walls, a massive brow ridge, a flat cheek region and a lower face that barely juts forward.

The paper reaches beyond Xujiayao. Its authors compared the anatomy with the Harbin skull known as Dragon Man and a jawbone from Penghu, off Taiwan, and they assigned most of East Asia’s late Middle Pleistocene fossils to the Denisovan lineage, including Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong.

The team also rejected the brain-size argument for Homo juluensis. Braincases in that group hold 1.8 to 1.9 quarts (1,700 to 1,800 milliliters) and the other East Asian fossils 1.2 to 1.5 quarts (1,120 to 1,420 milliliters), but modern humans alone span 1.15 to 2 quarts (1,090 to 1,880 milliliters).

If shape and molecules count together, the authors argued, Denisovans lived in East Asia from at least 300,000 to 45,000 years ago. The authors linked their disappearance from the region to a major migration of modern humans around 40,000 years ago.

The authors wrote that adding other skulls gives “a nearly complete picture of the cranial morphology of Denisovans.” That portrait is a composite.

Its account of a sloping forehead, square eye sockets and a broad nasal opening relies on facial bones from Harbin, Jinniushan, Hualongdong and Dali, and it also matches features predicted from Denisovan DNA.

Only Harbin among those four has molecular confirmation in the paper. Jinniushan, Dali and Hualongdong join the lineage on shape alone, and the authors note that the full set of traits does not appear together in any single specimen.

The protein evidence also has limits. It rests on one reliable variant, known from five reference individuals, and it comes from two of the 20 Xujiayao fossils. Within the Denisovan branch, individuals formed an unstable arrangement with probabilities below 50 percent.

A test for a variant specific to Penghu produced no reliable result, so the team placed Xujiayao only in a late Middle Pleistocene East Asian Denisovan population. The 1970s excavators left the bones with a site name, and a drill hole in each of two pieces has now added a lineage.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6385. Could Vitamin B12 Hold the Key to Treating a Rare Genetic Disorder?

A search for genes linked to lifespan uncovered an unexpected connection between RNA splicing, metabolism, and developmental disorders.

A mutation linked to a rare developmental disorder appears to interfere with more than the way cells process genetic instructions. Researchers discovered that it also disrupts vitamin B12-dependent metabolism in tiny roundworms. Supplying the vitamin restored key metabolic processes and corrected developmental abnormalities in the animals, raising questions about whether a similar approach could eventually help people.

The findings concern Verheij syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that causes developmental delays, growth problems, and short stature in children. The condition is associated with changes in a gene involved in RNA splicing, an essential process that prepares messenger RNA for protein production. During splicing, cells remove unnecessary sections of RNA and join the remaining pieces to form instructions that can be used to build proteins.

The discovery emerged from experiments with the roundworm C. elegans, a widely used model organism in biological research. Scientists were initially searching for genes that influence lifespan when they identified a mutation in a splicing-related gene associated with Verheij syndrome in humans. Worms carrying the mutation grew more slowly and remained unusually small, resembling some of the developmental problems seen in affected children.

Further genetic screening and metabolic analysis showed that the mutation altered biochemical pathways that depend on vitamin B12. These pathways support normal growth and cellular function. When researchers administered vitamin B12 to the affected worms, the disrupted metabolic processes returned to normal, and the animals’ developmental defects were corrected.

“We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism,” says Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. “Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12.”

To investigate whether similar metabolic disruptions occur in humans, the researchers examined publicly available data from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at University Hospital Cologne, to obtain blood samples from patients with Verheij syndrome. The analyses provided evidence that metabolic pathways affected in the worms may also be altered in people with the condition.

However, the results do not establish that vitamin B12 supplementation can treat Verheij syndrome in humans. Additional research is needed to determine whether the metabolic changes contribute directly to patients’ symptoms and whether correcting them could provide clinical benefits. The findings also suggest that metabolic dysfunction may deserve greater attention in other genetic disorders involving defective RNA splicing.

“Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide new insights into human diseases,” says Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. “A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term.”

Reference: “Vitamin B12 alleviates spliceosomopathy via phospholipid remodeling” by Jonathan Kölschbach, Hormos S. Dafsari, Emily Baum, Anna Löhrke, Chun Kew, Ivan Dikic, Wenming Huang and Adam Antebi, 7 August 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76295-9

#6384. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

#6382. An Egyptian villager working near his house discovered the buried remains of two colossal pharaoh statues

A villager's discovery in Egypt led archaeologists to two colossal royal statues, including a confirmed Ramesses II figure once about 28 feet tall.

A resident of Behbeit El-Hagar, a village in Egypt’s Gharbia Governorate, was working a plot he owns in front of his house. There he found a strange inscription on a stone block, and he reported it right away.

From there, a rescue excavation by Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities (SCA) uncovered the remains of two colossal royal statues. Egypt’s Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announced the finds on October 13, 2026.

One statue is confirmed as Ramesses II. Its head alone stands about 5.2 feet (1.6 meters) high.

Behbeit El-Hagar lies in the central Nile Delta. The village holds the ruins of a major temple to the goddess Isis, according to the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

The resident alerted the local antiquities inspectorate. Inspectors examined the stone and confirmed that it was an ancient artifact, and the SCA sent a specialist team to excavate the spot.

Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy praised the resident for reporting the stone immediately. He said public involvement is key to protecting Egypt’s heritage for future generations.

Fathy called the discovery an important addition to Egypt’s recent finds. In his view, it sheds further light on the history and archaeological significance of Behbeit El-Hagar.

The block that started the search is pink granite, about 4.3 feet (1.3 meters) long. Its hieroglyphs preserve two royal titles of Ramesses II.

One is Nesu-bity, or “King of Upper and Lower Egypt.” The other is Sa-Ra, or “Son of Ra.”

Dr. Hisham El-Leithy, secretary-general of the SCA, described the first statue. The king wears the Double Crown, which symbolized the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt.

The upper part of the statue’s back pillar also survives. It is inscribed with the king’s Horus name, Hor-ka-nakht-mery-maat, often rendered as “Strong bull, beloved of Maat.”

Based on the size of the head, El-Leithy estimated that the complete statue stood about 28 feet (8.5 meters) tall, including its base. The estimate rests on proportions, since only parts of that statue have been recovered.

Ramesses II, whose monuments include a Luxor obelisk now in Paris, reigned for 66 years. His rule, from about 1279 to 1213 B.C., fell within the 19th Dynasty of Egypt’s New Kingdom.

The second find is the main body of a royal statue, about 7.9 feet (2.4 meters) long. Its legs and base are missing.

This figure wears the nemes, the striped royal headcloth, and part of its top is lost. The face remains clear and well preserved.

Those features resemble the first statue’s, and archaeologists believe the second figure may also depict Ramesses II. That identification has not been confirmed.

The granite block lay roughly 3.3 feet (1 meter) north of this second statue.

Excavation and study will continue at the site, El-Leithy said. The goal is a clearer picture of the statues, the area’s history and its architectural development.

The Isis temple at Behbeit El-Hagar is much younger than Ramesses II. Nectanebo II, who ruled from 360 to 343 B.C., built most of it in dark granite, in a severe style typical of his dynasty’s Delta temples.

That work came roughly 850 years after Ramesses II’s reign ended. Nectanebo II decorated only one important chapel before the second Persian invasion of Egypt.

The temple probably replaced an earlier one begun in the 26th Dynasty. Ptolemy II later completed the sanctuary and chapels, and Ptolemy III added a hypostyle hall and the western facade.

The temple collapsed sometime after Ptolemy III and before the early third century A.D. Weak foundations may have played a part, and an earthquake, possibly in 24 B.C., may have brought it down.

Blocks from the temple have reached museums abroad. One granodiorite relief at the Met shows Nectanebo II offering incense and a collar to the god Osiris.

The ministry’s announcement does not connect the two statues to the Isis temple.

Ramesses II had statues of himself made across his empire. Among them are seated figures about 69 feet (21 meters) tall at Abu Simbel.

His mortuary temple, the Ramesseum, stood on the West Bank at Thebes, modern Luxor. One colossal seated figure there was carved from a single block of granite quarried near Aswan, according to the British Museum.

The surviving head and torso, now in London, measure just over 8.2 feet (2.5 meters). The complete seated figure would have reached roughly 23 feet (7 meters).

A red granite sphinx found at Memphis carries Ramesses II’s titles, but his sculptors reworked it from an earlier king’s monument. Flinders Petrie excavated it near the temple of Ptah in 1913.

The sphinx’s original owner was erased so thoroughly that he is unlikely ever to be identified. Ramesses II’s son and successor, Merenptah, later added his own cartouches to its shoulders.

The information was obtained from Egypt’s Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities.

#6381. Scientists Discover a Hidden Weakness in One of the Deadliest Cancers

Researchers have identified another potential approach to treating pancreatic cancer, with early experiments suggesting that blocking a protein could slow tumor growth and strengthen immune defenses.

Pancreatic tumors can be surrounded by tissue so dense that it compresses blood vessels, making it difficult for nutrients to reach cancer cells. Even under these conditions, the cells continue growing. How they obtain the materials needed to survive has remained an important question.

Researchers at Fox Chase Cancer Center have identified one way pancreatic cancer cells obtain cholesterol and other fats, known as lipids. Their study, published in Nature Cancer, also identified a protein that helps control this process and could offer a potential target for cancer treatment.

The research focused on pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the most common type of pancreatic cancer. These tumors contain large numbers of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), cells that produce and organize connective tissue. As CAFs and their collagen fibers expand, they can compress nearby blood vessels, restricting the tumor’s blood supply.

Despite contributing to this nutrient shortage, CAFs also help cancer cells overcome it.

“We found that CAFs can act as a source of these nutrients,” said Edna Cukierman, PhD, a professor and co-leader of the Cancer Signaling and Microenvironment Program at Fox Chase and co-senior author of the study. “Using laboratory and animal models, we discovered that CAF units acquire cholesterol from the bloodstream and transfer it to nearby pancreatic cancer cells through a process called trogocytosis”

Trogocytosis occurs when one cell takes small pieces of another cell’s membrane during direct contact. In this case, pancreatic cancer cells acquire pieces of CAF membranes containing cholesterol and other lipids that support their survival and growth.

The researchers discovered that this transfer depends on a protein called anoctamin 6 (ANO6), which helps prepare the CAF membrane for the exchange.

“These findings help explain how pancreatic cancer cells obtain essential nutrients despite the unusual structure of the pancreatic tumor microenvironment,” said Igor Astsaturov, MD, PhD, a professor at Fox Chase and co-senior author of the study. “Cancer-associated fibroblasts are not passive bystanders. They actively support tumor growth by transferring lipids to cancer cells.”

When researchers reduced or eliminated ANO6 in CAFs, the cells became less effective at supporting pancreatic cancer cell survival. In mouse models, tumors supported by CAFs with functional ANO6 grew substantially faster than those without functional ANO6.

The same nutrient transfer process also appeared to interfere with the immune system.

Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) are immune cells that recognize and kill cancer cells. When these T cells come into contact with CAFs, they can acquire membrane material containing cholesterol. Excess cholesterol in the tumor environment can contribute to T-cell exhaustion, making these immune cells less effective at fighting cancer.

“With Serge Fuchs, professor at the University of Pennsylvania and co-author on the paper, we were surprised to find that the same cellular mechanism can benefit the tumor in two ways – by supplying cancer cells with lipids while also weakening cancer-fighting T cells,” said Astsaturov. “Targeting ANO6 could potentially disrupt both of these tumor-supporting functions at the same time.”

In mouse models, blocking ANO6 reduced cholesterol accumulation in T cells within tumors and improved markers of their activity. Laboratory experiments also showed that T cells exposed to CAFs with reduced ANO6 were better able to kill cancer cells.

The researchers then tested whether drugs that interfere with ANO6-dependent activity could slow tumor growth. In mouse models, treatment with niclosamide or clofazimine significantly reduced tumor weight. Niclosamide also reduced cholesterol delivery to pancreatic cancer cells.

These findings suggest that targeting ANO6 could both restrict a nutrient source for pancreatic tumors and improve the immune response against them. However, the results remain preclinical, and further research is needed to determine whether selectively blocking ANO6 would work as a treatment in patients.

Trogocytosis is also only one of several ways pancreatic cancer cells may obtain lipids. The researchers suggest that the drugs tested could potentially help treat other difficult cancers, although that possibility requires further investigation.

“We believe our findings identify ANO6 as a potential therapeutic target that could simultaneously disrupt the nutrient supply supporting pancreatic cancer cells and reduce the immune-suppressive effects of the tumor microenvironment,” said Astsaturov.

The findings also build on nearly a decade of research into how the tissue surrounding pancreatic tumors supports cancer growth.

“Excitingly, reducing ANO6 expression also disrupted the stromal synapse-mimicry circuit we previously identified, which coordinates tumor nutritional support, CAF-unit metabolism, and immune suppression. These findings position ANO6 as the missing mechanistic link that unifies nearly a decade of discoveries by our team,” said Cukierman.

Reference: “ANO6-mediated trogocytosis of cancer-associated fibroblasts promotes pancreatic cancer cell growth and immune suppression” by Charline Ogier, Akino Mercy Charles Solomon, Elena Bondarenko, Zhijing Wu, Zhen Lu, Quoc Thang Bui, Mayura R. Deneka, Ralph Francescone, Anna C. Lilly, Alyssa Sipman, Jaye C. Gardiner, Tiffany Luong, Janusz Franco-Barraza, Aleksandr Dolskii, Mariia Dmitrieva, Kathy Q. Cai, Margret B. #6380. Voyager 1 went silent in deep space right before reaching a historic milestone of one ‘light day’ away from Earth

NASA briefly lost contact with Voyager 1 in October 2026. The signal returned just weeks before the spacecraft reaches a historic milestone.

On Oct. 18, 2026, the antennas of NASA’s Deep Space Network tried to pick up Voyager 1 during a scheduled contact and found nothing. A second attempt 24 hours later also failed.

The signal came back on Oct. 20, and the team at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California has kept in touch with the probe since then.

NASA schedules Nov. 18 as the day Voyager 1, already the farthest human-made object, reaches one light-day from Earth, according to JPL. They had not previously said what caused the October problems.

The Deep Space Network has large antennas at Goldstone in California, near Madrid in Spain and near Canberra in Australia. The largest dish at each site measures about 230 feet (70 meters) across.

Those antennas handled the two contact attempts in October. Mission controllers logged no detectable signal on Oct. 18 or Oct. 19.

Kareem Badaruddin, the Voyager mission manager at JPL, said the episode was new to his team. “This is the first time we’ve seen the spacecraft do something like this,” he said in the JPL statement.

He also said the mission has reached a stage where the team has “to expect the unexpected.” The probe has surprised its operators before, including the time it began talking through a radio system not used since 1981.

After contact returned, the team worked out that one group of thrusters on the spacecraft had gone offline and that a backup group had turned on.

The onboard computers carry instructions to make that swap by themselves when they detect a problem with the active thrusters.

JPL calls this kind of automatic reaction fault protection. It puts the probe in a safe, stable state and pauses normal operations so that engineers on the ground can study the problem.

In March 2025, engineers revived a set of roll thrusters that had stopped working in 2004.

Early in September, about six weeks before the probe dropped out of contact, JPL engineers sent the commands that turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and turned on three lower-power substitutes.

Inside the team, the job goes by the name Big Bang. The devices double as a source of warmth for the spacecraft, so JPL could not do them one at a time and all three changed at once.

Voyager 2 got the treatment first, and NASA reported on Aug. 4, 2026 that the swap there should keep three instruments powered for at least one more year. An instrument on Voyager 2 would otherwise have gone dark before the end of 2026.

Nothing in the Oct. 29 note ties the September commands to the thrusters.

Both probes run on radioisotope generators, which turn the heat from decaying plutonium into electricity. The output on each probe falls by about 4 watts a year and, with margins now thin, JPL has been shutting off whatever is not essential.

Ten science instruments went up on Voyager 1 in 1977. A NASA status page updated in April lists only two still running on it, the magnetometer and the plasma wave subsystem.

Controllers switched off the cosmic ray subsystem on Feb. 25, 2025, in one of a series of shutdowns meant to stretch the remaining power. The low-energy charged particle instrument was next, on April 17, 2026.

Without the Big Bang swap, another Voyager 1 instrument would likely have been turned off as early as summer 2027, JPL said.

Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, two weeks after its twin, passed Jupiter and Saturn, and entered interstellar space in August 2012. It is moving at about 38,000 miles per hour (61,155 kilometers per hour).

NASA’s light-day page sets the crossing on Nov. 18, when the probe will sit about 16.09 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from Earth.

Light covers the distance to the Moon in 1.3 seconds. Artemis II astronauts needed about three days for the same trip.

NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory explains how far away Voyager 1 is when it reaches one light-day from Earth. Credit: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

Voyager 2 took a different route so it could visit Uranus and Neptune, and NASA expects it to reach the same distance in November 2035. The nearest star system, Proxima Centauri, lies about 4.24 light-years away.

Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd described what the distance does to a conversation. “If you want to say ‘hello’ to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response,” she said in the JPL statement.

JPL’s Oct. 29 note does not say what knocked the thrusters offline, and engineers are still investigating. It also does not confirm that the thruster switch was what interrupted the signal.

The note does not name the three devices replaced in September or give the amount of power saved. It also says nothing about when the mission might end, although the team expects more surprises before summer 2027.

The light-day crossing itself will change nothing on board or around the spacecraft, JPL said. Its value lies in showing the length of the mission and the size of the distances involved.

At one light-day, a command sent from Goldstone, Madrid or Canberra needs a full day to reach Voyager 1. The answer needs another.

The information was obtained from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

This tiny inkwell contains an alphabetic inscription in ancient Etruscan, a language that has never been fully decoded.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The chicken-shaped, black-glazed vase has an abecedarium ‪—‬ an inscription with the 26 letters of the Etruscan alphabet in order.

What it is: A bird-shaped ceramic inkwell

This small terra-cotta vase, which is shaped like a cockerel or young male chicken with human feet, was discovered in central Italy and was made by the ancient Etruscans. The potter inscribed the Etruscan alphabet on the body of the chicken, giving modern researchers clues to a language that has never been fully deciphered.

The vase stands just over 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. The dark-black ceramic, known as bucchero, was made through a unique firing method that prevented the kiln from getting enough oxygen, which caused the clay to absorb carbon. Bucchero is considered the trademark Etruscan ceramic, and it was produced from the seventh to the fourth centuries B.C. by this pre-Roman society. It is unclear where the cockerel vase was originally found, but it may have been discovered in a grave in one of the many cemeteries that surround Viterbo, which was originally an Etruscan town about 50 miles (80 kilometers) northwest of modern-day Rome.

According to The Met, the vase may have been a portable inkwell used by an ancient Etruscan who was learning how to write. The cockerel's head was the stopper, and it was loosely attached to the body by a cord through a set of loops. The inscription on the body of the vase is known as an abecedarium ‪—‬ the sequential list of letters in an alphabet.

The Etruscan alphabet is well known, since it was adopted from a regional version of the Greek alphabet in the early eighth century B.C. There were 26 letters in the Etruscan alphabet, but one of them in this abecedarium is incorrect. A close look at the end of the alphabet shows that someone inscribed an S twice; the second one should look more like an X, according to The Met.

The terracotta cockerel vase was one of several ancient Etruscan artifacts that helped experts partially decode the mysterious ancient language, as it preserved the order of the letters in the early alphabet, archaeologist Gisela Richter wrote in a 1930 catalog of The Met's classical artifacts.

Thanks to the adoption of the Greek alphabet, it's possible to fully sound out the Etruscan language. But although more than 10,000 Etruscan inscriptions have been found, the language is still only partially understood because those inscriptions are short and any lengthy Etruscan literature that once existed has been lost.

#6377. Scientists got a much better look at endangered red pandas by putting cameras in trees

The red panda has a false thumb, and there's a good reason for that. To photograph a shy wild animal, researchers usually set up a motion-sensing camera near…

To photograph a shy wild animal, researchers usually set up a motion-sensing camera near the ground and wait for the animal to walk by. For red pandas, a camera placed near the ground misses a lot, because these endangered animals live mostly up in the trees.

At 19 sites in eastern Nepal, cameras about 16 feet (5 meters) up in trees took eight times as many pictures of red pandas as cameras near the ground. With cameras in the trees, researchers can watch an animal that is very hard to spot in the wild.

Sonam Tashi Lama of the Red Panda Network, a conservation group, led the work with Kathryn Bugler, James Ross, and Adrian Paterson at Lincoln University in New Zealand.

“Red pandas are very elusive,” Lama said. In eastern Nepal, oak trees are often covered in a reddish moss, and a red panda’s reddish fur blends into it. Researchers sometimes mistake pieces of moss for red pandas from a distance.

Lama said the camouflage helps protect red pandas from predators. Those predators likely include clouded leopards and common leopards, and sometimes yellow-throated martens, tree-climbing animals that usually hunt in pairs.

The same camouflage makes red pandas hard to study. Their behavior in the wild hasn’t been studied much, because the animals are so difficult to find and follow.

Researchers in earlier studies watched red pandas in person, fitted them with GPS tracking collars, or looked for their droppings. Lama’s team tested whether cameras could help, and whether they work better near the ground or in the trees.

From late 2017 to mid-2018, the team set up 19 pairs of motion-sensing cameras, known as camera traps, in the forests of eastern Nepal. Each pair stayed in place for at least a month.

The team picked trees that red pandas were already using. Fresh droppings and feeding marks showed which trees those were. Local people called Forest Guardians, who monitor red pandas for the Red Panda Network, helped choose the sites.

One camera in each pair was mounted on a tree trunk, about 16 inches (40 centimeters) above the ground. The other was placed up in the branches, about 16 feet above the ground.

There’s a reason for that height. Red pandas leave their droppings at regular spots in trees, and those spots are about 16 feet up on average.

Together, the cameras took almost 60,000 pictures. More than three-quarters of them showed no animal at all. Moving leaves and the heat of sunlight can set off a camera’s sensor, and that happened far more often in the trees.

Red pandas appeared in only 903 pictures, at 11 of the 19 sites. The tree cameras took 807 of those pictures, and the ground cameras took 96.

The team also counted how many separate times a red panda showed up. Tree cameras recorded 38 appearances. Ground cameras recorded 21. But a single appearance in a tree could produce a long series of pictures.

In one case, the team wrote, a tree camera recorded a single red panda over a period of 2 hours and 18 minutes. In that time, the animal slept in different positions, groomed itself, and explored its surroundings and the camera.

Red pandas sometimes investigated the tree cameras, but they didn’t touch them. One camera, aimed down a tree trunk, recorded a red panda climbing down headfirst.

The pictures also showed red pandas active at all hours of the day and night. The animals were busiest between 4 and 6 in the morning. They eat constantly, Lama said, taking only short naps between meals of bamboo.

Putting a camera in a tree is harder than setting one up near the ground. Reaching a tree camera takes a ladder or climbing gear. The team wrote that each one also took about 30 minutes longer to set up and to check.

The Forest Guardians are skilled tree climbers, Lama said. Tree cameras also took many more pictures with no animal in them, which gave the team more pictures to sort through.

Even so, the team wrote that the extra effort is worth it, because wild red pandas have been so difficult to observe. They recommended that researchers who want to monitor red pandas mount cameras in trees, about 16 feet up.

At that height, a camera can show whether red pandas are present, when they are active, how they behave, and possibly which predators are nearby. At one site in this study, a marten was photographed in a tree that a red panda often visited.

Ground cameras still have a use, the team wrote. They can record red pandas, but they are better suited to recording the other mammals that live on the forest floor.

Pictures from the tree cameras were clear enough to show the markings on each red panda’s face. Those markings differ from one animal to the next, so researchers can use them to tell red pandas apart.

Local populations of red pandas in Nepal are very small, typically 20 to 50 animals. Lama’s team didn’t use the pictures to estimate how many red pandas live in the study area. In future studies, the team wrote, the face markings could make that kind of estimate possible.

Biologists often estimate how many animals live in an area by learning to recognize individual animals, then recording how often they see the same ones again. The method is called mark-recapture.

The next question is whether that method works for red pandas. To make the animals easier to identify, the team suggested aiming cameras so they capture a red panda’s whole body.

The full study was published in the journal Wildlife Society Bulletin.

#6376. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

#6374. Scientists Just Found a Key Ingredient for Superconductivity at Room Temperature

Researchers have discovered that a key requirement for superconductivity can persist even at room temperature.

Scientists searching for a superconductor that works at room temperature have identified a potential way forward. New research from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich shows that electrons can form the pairs needed for superconductivity even at room temperature. The findings, published in Science, suggest that a different requirement may be preventing these materials from conducting electricity without resistance.

The key appears to be how paired electrons behave collectively. Although the pairs can survive at much higher temperatures than previously understood, they must also act in a coordinated way for superconductivity to emerge.

Electrical resistance causes energy to be lost as heat whenever current passes through an ordinary conductor. This is useful in a toaster, where resistance heats a metal wire until it glows, but undesirable in power transmission and electronic devices. Superconductors eliminate electrical resistance, potentially enabling more efficient energy storage, levitating trains, and advanced quantum computers.

The obstacle is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C (-436°F), often using expensive liquid helium. Superconductivity was first discovered in 1911, and researchers made major progress in the mid-1980s when they identified materials that could become superconducting at temperatures around -173°C (-279°F). Yet these higher-temperature superconductors presented a mystery: the established theory explaining conventional superconductivity could not account for their behavior.

“We don’t understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all,” says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. “And if you don’t understand it, you can’t systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal.”

Superconductivity requires two essential conditions. First, electrons must form partnerships known as Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated quantum state called phase coherence. Without both conditions, a material cannot sustain superconductivity.

In conventional superconductors, electron pairing and phase coherence emerge together as the material cools below a critical temperature. The new research shows that these processes can occur separately in high-temperature superconductors. Electron pairs can form and remain stable at temperatures far above the point where electrical resistance disappears, including at room temperature.

“This is really good news,” says Swart. “We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren’t possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether.”

The findings indicate that the interaction binding electrons into pairs can remain sufficiently strong at room temperature. This shifts attention toward phase coherence, which may be the limiting factor preventing superconductivity at higher temperatures.

“The ‘glue’ that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature,” says Swart. “This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck.”

The researchers have not demonstrated room-temperature superconductivity, but their results help narrow the search for what is missing. Swart plans to investigate how phase coherence develops and what prevents electron pairs from achieving it at higher temperatures.

“If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures.”

Reference: “Equivalence of pseudogap and pairing energy in a cuprate high-temperature superconductor” by Jiasen Niu, Maialen Ortego Larrazabal, Thomas Gozlinski, Yudai Sato, Koen M. Bastiaans, Tjerk Benschop, Jian-Feng Ge, Yaroslav M. Blanter, Genda Gu, Ingmar Swart and Milan P. Allan, 5 November 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.adt3444

However, attempting to “understand” it using the perturbative language of the BCS paradigm is to go nowhere (doomed to reach a dead end). The collapse of phase coherence is essentially the thermal destruction of topological order; what is required is the language of geometry and topology, not Feynman diagrams and coupling constants.

It is suggested that researchers attempt to reformulate “phase coherence” using a topological order parameter (rather than a traditional one) and examine the excitation and unbinding temperatures of vortex-antivortex pairs. This approach may be closer to the essence of the phenomenon than merely tracking “pairing strength.” This is a perfect counterexample—even the most astute mainstream researchers, constrained by their paradigm, can only “approach” the correct answer without ever truly arriving at it. This is precisely the reason why geometric realism needs to be introduced.

Mainstream physics has developed a highly instrumentalized, terminologized, and project-driven research ecology: (1) Large-scale facilities need to continuously generate news, and therefore tend to adopt expressions such as “unlocking,” “hidden,” “strange,” and “quantum breakthrough”; (2) Peer review tends to reward publishable labels for new phenomena rather than deeper geometric unification; (3) “Quantum materials” have gradually become a tool for funding allocation and journal classification, with their conceptual boundaries being continually stretched; (4) Experimental precision keeps rising, yet much work remains at the level of phenomenological classification, lacking a fundamental reconstruction of phase fields, vortex topology, and fluid geometry. This has become a brazenly shameless state of affairs in mainstream physics.

Einstein’s sorrowful silhouette has faded into the distance. But his intuition, his persistence, his belief in “local realism”, has finally found its rightful home in the framework of Topological Vortex Theory (TVT). Einstein was not a failed prophet, but a true physicist misunderstood by his era.

However, the mainstream framework treats “pairing” and “phase coherence” as two separable steps, an approach that is itself questionable. From the perspective of Topological Vortex Theory (TVT), superconductivity is essentially a long-range ordered state of topological vortex structures within the electron fluid. Pairing and coherence are never two distinct entities but rather two facets of the same vortex structure. To separate them in search of a “bottleneck” is akin to asking “which is more important: the rotation of a vortex or its overall motion”—the question itself is flawed.

A deeper issue lies in the “glue” metaphor. The mainstream narrative implies that electrons require some localized attractive force to “bind” them, which is typical particle-based thinking. In reality, the correlation between electrons arises from the geometric constraints of the fluid medium, not from some “glue” pulling them together. #6373. Bed bugs aren’t just a poverty problem, new study reveals

Genetic research across three states challenges the idea that persistent bed bug populations are confined to disadvantaged neighborhoods.

There’s a stubborn myth that bed bugs are a poverty problem.

In this view, infestations are confined to neglected housing, overcrowded apartments, and neighborhoods where residents can’t afford an exterminator.

New genetic research suggests the reality is more democratic – and more unsettling.

Bed bug reservoir populations, the persistent colonies that seed new infestations across a city, turn up in neighborhoods with both high and low social vulnerability.

The study was led by Cari Lewis from the Los Alamos National Laboratory and Warren Booth from Virginia Tech.

It is the first to combine population genomics with census-derived measures of social vulnerability to map how bed bug populations are structured across American cities.

Bed bugs have been living alongside humans for a very long time. The human-adapted lineage of Cimex lectularius split from its bat-associated ancestor roughly 245,000 years ago.

Bed bugs can’t fly or jump. Human-associated populations shelter indoors and spread by hitchhiking on our belongings.

“Bed bugs are expert hitchhikers,” Booth said. “They readily move into luggage, backpacks, purses, clothing, and other personal belongings.”

Adults are about the size of an apple seed. Immature stages are much smaller.

“Their ability to hide in tiny crevices makes accidental transport remarkably common,” Booth added.

The researchers collected specimens from 195 infestations between 2018 and 2022 across three states: Oklahoma, Illinois, and Ohio.

They extracted DNA and sequenced it using a technique called ddRADseq. This method surveys thousands of single nucleotide polymorphisms scattered across the genome.

Then they used network analysis and principal components analysis to identify genetically distinct populations within each state.

The genetic signatures were striking: Oklahoma’s bed bugs fell into seven distinct clusters, Ohio into ten and Illinois five.

Within each state, genetic differentiation between clusters was significant despite some clusters spanning huge geographic distances. Oklahoma’s most distant infestations were nearly 200 miles apart.

Geographic proximity alone did not explain the genetic relationships between infestations.

“Rather than spreading simply between nearby locations, these populations are connected through networks of human movement and the transport of personal belongings, similar to the models used to examine disease transmission within populations,” Booth explained.

The researchers layered their genetic data onto the CDC’s Social Vulnerability Index.

This standardized measure scores census tracts across four themes: socioeconomic status, household characteristics, racial and ethnic minority status, and housing type and transportation.

In Oklahoma and Illinois, certain genetic clusters were associated with higher or lower social vulnerability.

But the reservoir populations – the genetically cohesive groups that persist over time and keep seeding new infestations – showed up across the entire spectrum.

They were found in rich neighborhoods and poor ones, in multi-unit housing and single-family homes.

In Ohio, no significant association between genetic clusters and any vulnerability measure was detected at all.

“A key finding of the research was the identification of reservoir populations: bed bug populations that persist over time and contribute to the spread of infestations beyond communities in which they are established,” Booth said.

“Importantly, these reservoirs of bed bugs occur across the socioeconomic spectrum, challenging the misconception that bed bugs are primarily a problem of disadvantaged communities.”

The genetic data revealed something else about bed bug biology. These populations are extremely inbred.

Average inbreeding coefficients were high across all three states – up to 0.353 in Illinois.

Estimated effective population sizes averaged just 3.5 to 5.5 across the three states. This genetic measure is not a count of the breeding bugs present.

Each infestation essentially starts from a handful of founders, reproduces in near-isolation, and builds its own genetically distinct colony.

The bugs don’t need large populations or high genetic diversity to establish and spread.

A few hitchhikers in a suitcase are plenty enough.

The insects are also increasingly resistant to the chemicals designed to kill them.

“Many bed bug populations are resistant to products that were once highly effective, especially pyrethroid-based insecticides,” Booth said.

“When infestations survive treatment, they continue to reproduce, spread, and increase the likelihood of additional introductions elsewhere.”

Detection is another problem. “Not all people who get bitten by bed bugs react to them,” Booth said.

Some people only discover they have an infestation when black spots start appearing on white bed sheets.

“That’s because they feed and then defecate and a little blood comes out,” he said. By that point, the colony may already be well established and spreading through wall voids to neighboring units.

If reservoir populations span the socioeconomic spectrum, then targeting pest management at disadvantaged neighborhoods alone won’t work.

The reservoirs that keep reintroducing bed bugs into treated areas are scattered across the entire urban landscape.

Booth advocates coordinated communitywide control, using early detection and infestation mapping to tackle bed bugs as a shared problem.

Management would focus on “simultaneous inspections and treatments of connected units and buildings, reducing re-infestation from neighboring sources.”

Regional policy differences already hint at what this might look like. Chicago has implemented landlord reporting requirements, education programs, and mandatory treatment protocols.

The study didn’t directly test whether Chicago’s regulations affect infestation patterns.

Yet, the finer-scale genetic structure detected in Illinois suggests that denser management and policy infrastructure may shape how bed bug populations organize and spread.

The research is published in the journal Parasites & Vectors.

In a key coastal area of Peru, violence was low despite the practice of human sacrifice.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Despite engaging in human sacrifice, the people who lived in the Lambayeque Valley of northern Peru had low levels of violence, a new study of their remains finds.

Human sacrifice occurred in the valley over the millennia. It's thought that at least some of these mass sacrifices were attempts to appease the gods in the wake of El Niño, a periodic weather phenomenon that can lead to intense rains and flooding in Peru and droughts in other parts of South and Central America.

"We have one example at the site of Sicán where around [A.D.] 1050/1100, around 200 individuals were killed and ritualistically buried during an intense El Niño event," study co-author Haagen Klaus, an anthropology professor at George Mason University in Virginia, told Live Science in an email.

Other human sacrifice findings include more than 200 children found near the modern-day town of Huanchaco who were sacrificed sometime between 600 and 800 years ago, possibly during an El Niño.

However, despite the occurrence of human sacrifice, levels of violence unrelated to sacrifice were actually quite low in the Lambayeque Valley. In the study, scientists analyzed the skeletal remains of 1,519 people from the Lambayeque Valley who lived between roughly 1500 B.C. and A.D. 1800, and whose remains were preserved enough to detect signs of violent trauma, including interpersonal violence.

A skull showing blunt force trauma that dates to the Chimu period, roughly 1375 to 1490.

Of these skeletons, "only 25 (1.6%) exhibited traumatic lesions consistent with interpersonal conflict, and 77 exhibited post-cranial traumatic lesions consistent with accidental trauma (5.1%)," Klaus and co-author Thomas Snyder, a bioarchaeologist at New York University, wrote in the paper, which was published Nov. 8 in the journal Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

The team didn't find any link between a person's sex and violence, they noted. The findings mean that despite the presence of human sacrifice, the amount of violence unrelated to sacrifice was low. This leaves a question: Why?

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A healed fracture on the left leg of a person who lived sometime between 1000 to 650 B.C. The fracture may have been from an accident.

"Ritual violence may have alleviated non-ritual violence by creating spaces where social tensions could get worked out in a few different ways," Klaus said.

It's important to remember that other areas of Peru also practiced human sacrifice but didn't have the same low levels of interpersonal violence. Klaus noted that areas in the Peruvian highlands sometimes had higher rates of interpersonal violence. In their paper, Klaus and Snyder noted that societies that originated in the highlands, such as the Tiwanaku, Wari and Inca had to grapple with poorer soils and cold temperatures, and these challenges may have been a factor in increasing the levels of interpersonal violence.

The "evidence of sub-lethal and lethal violence forceful enough to break bone is significantly higher in some areas of Peru's highlands," Klaus said. He and Snyder noted in their paper that the inhabitants of the Lambayeque Valley may have had better access to marine and water resources, such as seafood and rivers that could be used for agricultural irrigation, than those who lived in highland areas. Access to these resources may have helped alleviate interpersonal violence in the valley by providing more food resources, they wrote.

Aside from practicing human sacrifice, people in the valley may have engaged in other practices that helped lower levels of interpersonal violence, researchers who were not involved in the new study told Live Science.

Environmental conditions may have helped reduce conflict or there could be "really unusual cultural practices in this region of avoiding or mediating conflict — both between and within groups," Elizabeth Arkush, an anthropology professor at the University of Pittsburgh, said in an email.

Constanza Ceruti, an anthropologist and explorer with the National Geographic Society, said in an email that she's glad that researchers are studying human sacrifices "after decades of being ignored as a taboo topic in academic discussion." She praised the study’s large sample size and noted that human sacrifice is a "phenomenon primarily associated [with] the manipulation and concentration of power by elites."

Jordi Rivera Prince, an anthropology professor at Tulane University, said that the findings dovetail with her excavations in the region, where she has "found little evidence of violent trauma during the Salinar (400-200 BCE), a period of great social change in the Andes."

Weston McCool, an archaeology professor at Cal Poly, said in an email that the newly published paper "is an interesting study that provides additional evidence for a sharp break in patterns of violence between the Andean coast and highlands." He noted that it "supports the hypothesis that coastal populations were buffered from terrestrial environmental downturns in ways that highland populations were not. The nature of that resilience, however, remains an important question for future research."

Snyder, T. J., & Klaus, H. D. (2026). Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru. Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, 5, 1889466. https://doi.org/10.3389/fearc.2026.1889466

He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6371. A Natural “Varnish” May Explain How 37,000-Year-Old Cave Art Survived

A new technique uses UV light to reveal a natural mineral varnish that may have helped preserve Chauvet Cave’s 37,000-year-old charcoal drawings.

About 37,000 years ago, Paleolithic people entered a limestone cave in southeastern France and drew the animals around them, including cave bears, cave lions, bison, and horses. An ancient rockfall later sealed away the artwork, leaving it undiscovered until the 1990s. Today, Chauvet Cave holds some of the oldest artwork in existence, along with clues to how the cave itself helped preserve it.

Getting close to those clues requires care. The site is so historically important and fragile that its location is kept secret and access is secured behind a huge steel door. Inside, prehistoric footprints lie in front of the artwork. Researchers examining the walls must also protect these traces of the people who once walked through the cave.

Researcher Philippe Walter describes the purpose of that painstaking work. “We examine every piece of evidence to decode the techniques of prehistoric artists and understand how the paintings have been preserved over time.”

In a study reported in ACS Omega, Walter and his colleagues investigated the charcoal drawings without touching the cave walls. They focused on mineral deposits that had formed over the artwork, looking for evidence of how the drawings were created and how the cave’s geology may have contributed to their preservation.

To work around the fragile footprints, the team placed a portable spectrometer on a protective walkway about 8 feet (2.5 meters) from the wall. This instrument measures light, allowing the researchers to examine materials from a distance.

Their approach used ultraviolet, or UV, fluorescence spectroscopy, a technique researchers have used to reveal fluorescent mineral deposits invisible to the naked eye. Certain materials emit light when exposed to UV illumination. By shining a UV beam onto the wall and analyzing the resulting glow, the team could investigate both the mineral deposits and the pigments in the artwork.

Two different colors offered clues to what had happened on the cave walls:

“Our methodology is much like forensic investigation: We examine every piece of evidence to decode the techniques of prehistoric artists and understand how the paintings have been preserved over time,” says Walter.

The team anticipates applications beyond cave art, from forensic science to monitoring biofilms aboard the International Space Station. Biofilms are communities of microorganisms that grow on surfaces. A project applying the technique to monitoring them aboard the station is already underway.

Reference: “In Situ Ultraviolet Fluorescence Spectroscopy for the Characterization of Translucent Calcite Coatings over Prehistoric Cave Art” by Yohan Boulard, Thiéry Guillou, Carole Fritz, Gilles Tosello, Maguy Jaber and Philippe Walter, 29 September 2026, ACS Omega. DOI: 10.1021/acsomega.6c05061

The authors acknowledge funding from the French Ministry of Culture, the French National Centre for Scientific Research (Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique), and Sorbonne University.

Disclosure: One of the authors is a founder of Lumentis, a company developing imaging instruments for historical artwork analysis.

#6370. Rose-colored rock found in the Sahara holds a rare piece of ancient Mars

A rose-colored meteorite found in the Sahara is a piece of ancient Martian crust that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago.

Although most of the surface of Mars is ancient rock, most Martian meteorites that land on Earth are young.

Found in the Sahara Desert in 2022, a rose-colored stone is an exception. It’s a piece of the planet’s early crust that formed at least 4.1 billion years ago.

Scientists rarely get to study a sample of the crust Mars had when it was young. The stone is called Teghaza 001, after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered.

Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California led the new study.

“It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique,” she said. “One of the paper’s reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars.”

The rock weighs nearly 2 pounds (800 grams). It’s one of roughly 435 known meteorites from Mars, and the new study is a first description of it rather than a full accounting.

Like every Martian meteorite, Teghaza 001 was blasted off the planet’s surface by an impact and later landed on Earth.

Collectors often find meteorites in deserts and snowy plains, where they stand out against the bare landscape.

Researchers at the University of New Mexico first identified the rock as Martian by checking its oxygen.

Oxygen atoms come in slightly different forms, called isotopes, and the mix of those forms differs from one planet to the next. Teghaza 001’s mix matched the mix in other Martian meteorites.

Scientists also confirm a Martian origin by comparing a meteorite’s minerals and chemistry with data from NASA missions, including the Viking landers and the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers.

At first, Teghaza 001 looked like a shergottite, the most common kind of meteorite from Mars.

Liu studies planetary samples and has seen plenty of those, so she almost passed on the chance to examine it. She looked anyway and found odd textures and unusual minerals she hadn’t seen before.

Liu and her colleagues found zircon crystals in the meteorite. Zircon records clues about how a rock formed, and geologists use it to date a sample precisely.

François Tissot, a coauthor at Caltech, helped the team use a dating method his group developed. Some dating methods require dissolving the sample being analyzed.

Tissot’s method instead measures single mineral grains on the surface of a piece smaller than a fingernail, so most of a rare rock stays intact for future studies.

“Right now, we are one of very few labs in the world able to perform this kind of age-dating, and the first to date such an ancient Martian meteorite,” Tissot said.

“Our hope is to pave the way for dating even more Martian meteorites, or samples returned from other planets, their moons, and asteroids.”

Liu was shocked by the results. Water on Mars had changed the rock sometime around 4.1 billion years ago, which suggests the rock itself formed even earlier.

Only two other Martian meteorites found on Earth are counted among the most ancient. One of them, ALH84001, is about the same age but is made almost entirely of one mineral.

The third, nicknamed Black Beauty, is made of small fragments of volcanic rock.

Teghaza 001’s mix of minerals formed as molten rock cooled slowly into crust. Later, water moving underground changed some of them.

That mix matches what NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter has observed in the heavily cratered southern highlands of Mars.

The rock’s exact birthplace on Mars remains unknown, but the team identified several locations that match its minerals and chemistry.

Lee Saper, the study’s second author, did the research as a postdoctoral scholar at JPL and is now a scientist at NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley.

“This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before. It records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water,” Saper said.

The water that reacted with Teghaza 001 was enriched in oxygen-18, an isotope with two more neutrons than the most common form.

Clues in the oxygen isotopes, the texture, and the chemistry of the rock’s minerals point to an active water cycle on early Mars.

A second study, published in June in Science Advances and led by Saper, measured water in the meteorite’s minerals.

It found that water on Mars about 4.1 billion years ago held at least roughly twice the share of heavy hydrogen that Earth’s seawater does.

The authors wrote that this result supports models in which young Mars lost hydrogen to space quickly.

So far, Liu, Saper and their colleagues have described the rock in broad terms. Later studies of it could help show how water and rock interacted on ancient Mars.

“We’ve only scratched the surface,” Liu said.

Liu and her coauthors now want to see what other research teams can learn from Teghaza 001.

The full study was published in the journal Science.
